title: Sally Goodin
description: 'Sally Goodin' has a claim to being the first commercial country music recording in history. On June 30 and July 1, 1922, Texas fiddler Eck Robertson (1887–1975) and Henry Gilliland traveled to Victor Records in New York City — legend has it they showed up uninvited after performing at a Confederate Veterans' reunion in Richmond — and recorded several sides. Robertson's solo recording of 'Sallie Gooden' on July 1 was released by Victor later that year, predating the Fiddlin' John Carson and Vernon Dalhart recordings often cited as country music's commercial beginnings. 'Sally Goodin' itself is a Texas contest fiddle showcase, built around a simple base melody that expands into a cascading series of variations. The tune was a competitive vehicle — Robertson used it to demonstrate his technique, particularly his facility in the high register and his command of string crossings — and it became the standard by which Texas-style contest fiddling was measured. Ralph Peer, who would later record the Carter Family and Jimmie Rodgers, supervised the session. The name may refer to a real woman in Robertson's community or simply be a rhyme-placeholder common in folk naming.

Don't rush — Eck Robertson played it with absolute authority, not with panic. Listen to the 1922 Victor recording if you can; it's the original template.

title: Fire on the Mountain
description: One of the most-played tunes in all of American old-time music, 'Fire on the Mountain' appears in American fiddle collections from the late 19th century and was almost certainly in oral circulation for decades before that. The image of fire on the mountain — visible across vast distances in the days before electric light, signaling danger or celebration — was a powerful metaphor in a culture where the mountains themselves defined the horizon. Early recordings by mountain string bands in the 1920s and 30s cemented its place as a session anchor. The pentatonic structure in A major makes it nearly impossible to play a wrong note on an in-tune fiddle, which is why it's among the first tunes beginners learn — but its rhythmic drive and forward momentum reward advanced players who discover what they can do inside those simple bones. Bill Monroe, Flatt and Scruggs, and Tommy Jarrell all recorded versions, each bringing a distinct interpretation to the same elemental melody.

title: Old Joe Clark
description: Named for a real person — Joseph Clark, born September 18, 1839, in Clay County, Kentucky — 'Old Joe Clark' is one of the most universally known tunes in the Appalachian tradition. Clark served in the 7th Kentucky Infantry (Union) during the Civil War, discharged in 1862 due to disability, and returned to the eastern Kentucky mountains where his name became attached to a body of floating comic and satirical verses. The tune itself is almost certainly older than the man, adapted from earlier dance music and given Clark's name when the local community found the verses irresistible. By the early 20th century it had spread across the mountains, collected in multiple states with dozens of verse variants. Cecil Sharp gathered versions in the 1910s. 'Old Joe Clark had a yellow cat / She would neither sing nor pray / She stuck her head in the buttermilk jar / And washed her sins away' is among the most memorable. The tune crossed into bluegrass and remains one of the first tunes any beginner learns. Bill Monroe, Doc Watson, and countless others recorded it. Its A major setting — simple, driving, pentatonic — is nearly universally playable and singable.

title: Shady Grove
description: One of the most haunting tunes in the Appalachian repertoire, 'Shady Grove' was first published in the Journal of American Folklore in 1915 but almost certainly predates that collection by decades. The melody shares deep DNA with the English ballad 'Matty Groves' (documented as early as 1613) and surfaces in an American manuscript as far back as 1786 in 'Henry Beck's Flute Book' — making it one of the oldest documented folk melodies on American soil. The tune's emotional grip comes from its Dorian mode: E Dorian in most American versions creates a feeling that hovers between major and minor, never fully landing in either, which gives 'Shady Grove' its characteristically bittersweet longing. The text follows the floating-verse tradition of Appalachian song: the 'shady grove' is a place of meeting, courtship, and loss — specific enough to feel real, vague enough to hold every listener's version. Jean Ritchie's recordings brought it to the folk revival. Doc Watson, Clarence Ashley, and the Grateful Dead all recorded it, cementing its status as one of the few Appalachian tunes with genuine crossover life.

title: Cripple Creek
description: Often the first tune a beginner fiddler learns, 'Cripple Creek' runs deeper than its reputation as a starter tune suggests. Named for Cripple Creek in Wythe County, Virginia — a real stream, not the Colorado gold rush town — the tune has been in continuous oral circulation since at least the late 1800s, with a documented reference in the Journal of American Folklore in 1915 and a version collected by Cecil Sharp in 1917 from Kentucky singers. Fiddlin' John Carson recorded it in 1923 in one of the earliest documented old-time recordings. The tune belongs to the broader family of creek and river songs — 'Going Down to Cripple Creek, going in a run / Going down to Cripple Creek to have a little fun' — where the creek is a place of escape, courtship, and release from daily labor. Its A-major setting and pentatonic skeleton make it one of the most accessible tunes in the tradition while its rhythmic drive keeps it compelling at any tempo. Bill Monroe, Earl Scruggs, and Don Reno all recorded it, carrying it deep into the bluegrass canon.

title: Blackberry Blossom
description: Popularized in the 1920s and 30s but likely older in origin. 'Blackberry Blossom' belongs to the category of 'decorated' tunes — its flowing melody invites ornamentation in a way that simpler breakdowns do not. The tune crossed from Old-Time into early bluegrass, becoming a vehicle for virtuosic picking. Flatt & Scruggs and later Doc Watson helped cement its place in American acoustic music.

title: Whiskey Before Breakfast
description: Despite its lighthearted title, 'Whiskey Before Breakfast' is a tune of real melodic beauty. Its origins are obscure — it appears in neither O'Neill's nor most early American collections — suggesting it may be a 20th-century composition that achieved the status of a traditional tune through widespread adoption. It has become a jam session standard across Old-Time and Celtic traditions, valued for its singable melody and clean structure.

title: Arkansas Traveler
description: The 'Arkansas Traveler' comes with one of the most specific and entertaining origin stories in American folk music. Around 1840, Colonel Sandford C. 'Sandy' Faulkner (1803–1874), a Kentucky-born cotton planter and Arkansas politician, got lost while campaigning through the Ozark back country. He stopped at a log cabin and found the settler initially unhelpful — until Faulkner, an accomplished fiddler, recognized the tune the man was struggling with and completed the second part of it. The settler instantly transformed from surly stranger to gracious host. The story became a comic dialogue about Yankee vs. Southern manners, city vs. country, traveler vs. local — and the tune became its soundtrack. Albert Fay published the tune and its dialogue sketch in 1847; it was one of the first pieces of music to be attributed to a specific Arkansas source. By the Civil War, 'Arkansas Traveler' was known across America. Thomas Hart Benton painted the famous scene in 1959. The tune has been recorded by more artists than can be counted and remains one of the most recognized American folk melodies in the world.

At jams, keep it simple and emphasize the call-and-response quality.

title: Soldier's Joy
description: Documented in print as early as 1780 in Thompson's 'Compleat Collection,' Soldier's Joy may derive from an English country dance called 'The King's Head.' Laudanum (opium) was once nicknamed 'soldier's joy,' lending the tune a darker folk etymology. It spread across the American South through the 18th-century fiddle tradition and remains the most commonly played tune at Old-Time jam sessions worldwide.

title: Kitchen Girl
description: A reel of uncertain origin that has circulated in Appalachian and Celtic traditions, 'Kitchen Girl' evokes the social world of early 20th-century rural households where music was made in the kitchen during informal gatherings. The domestic setting — the kitchen as the social heart of the home — was a common site for music-making in pre-radio Appalachian communities. The tune was collected in multiple versions across the Southern mountains.

title: John Henry
description: John Henry's story — a Black steel-driver who raced a steam drill through a Virginia mountain and won, then died with his hammer in his hand — is one of the central myths of American industrial labor. The historical event probably occurred at the Lewis Tunnel on the Chesapeake and Ohio Railway in Summers County, West Virginia, around 1870–1872. Whether a real John Henry died there is disputed; what is indisputable is that the song and the myth spread through the railroad gangs of the late 19th century with the speed of fire. By the 1920s it had been collected across the South in hundreds of versions. The fiddle tune version captures the relentless hammering rhythm of the original work song in A minor — the driving downbeats, the unrelenting forward motion, the sense of a man working against a force that will outlast him. Guy Johnson's 1929 book 'John Henry: Tracking Down a Negro Legend' was the first scholarly treatment.
notes: Feel the hammer in your bow arm. The A minor key and relentless rhythm should convey effort and power — this is not an easy or gentle tune. The steady quarter-note feel in the A part should sound like hammer blows. The B part provides rhythmic contrast. At medium-fast tempo, the tune acquires the inexorable quality of work that cannot stop. Don't rush; real hammer work has a steady, sustainable rhythm. Emphasize the downbeats.

title: Angeline the Baker
description: Stephen Foster published 'Angelina Baker' in 1850 for the Christy Minstrels, writing it at a moment of intense national debate over the Fugitive Slave Act and the expansion of slavery. The original was a sentimental song in minstrel dialect about an enslaved woman separated from her lover by sale — a subject Foster returned to repeatedly, using the conventions of minstrel performance to express what the historical record suggests was genuine grief about the institution of slavery. The fiddle tune adapted from Foster's melody stripped the lyrics and transformed the song into a dance tune, a common fate for Foster compositions that spread virally through 19th-century America. By the Civil War era, 'Angeline the Baker' was circulating as an instrumental far removed from the Christy Minstrels stage. By the time it reached the 20th-century old-time revival, it had accumulated over 50 years of folk transmission and dozens of regional variants. It appears in numerous early fiddle recordings and remains a standard in both old-time and bluegrass sessions.

title: Sandy River Belle
description: One of the cornerstone tunes of the Round Peak style and the Tommy Jarrell repertoire, 'Sandy River Belle' takes its name from the Sandy River, which flows through Surry and Forsyth Counties in North Carolina — the heart of the musical region that Jarrell, Fred Cockerham, and their contemporaries called home. Tommy Jarrell (1901–1985) played with a bow arm power and directness that defined Round Peak fiddle for generations of revival players who came to study with him in the 1970s; 'Sandy River Belle' exemplifies that style at its most characteristic. The tune's A major setting and two-part structure are conventional; what's unconventional is the way Jarrell's bowing — heavy, close to the bridge, with deliberate drone-string use — transforms a simple melody into a full-body rhythmic experience. It was recorded by Jarrell and documented in the Field Recorders' Collective archive.
tags: tommy jarrell, surry county, north carolina, round peak
notes: Learn the Round Peak approach before you attempt this tune: bow close to the bridge, use the full length of the bow, let the lower strings drone. Tommy Jarrell's recordings are the mandatory reference — listen until you understand not just the notes but the bow weight and the rhythmic feel. The A part drives forward; the B part has a slight lift. Don't clean it up; the roughness and directness are the music, not defects to be corrected.

title: Cold Frosty Morning
description: A signature tune of the Round Peak, North Carolina tradition, 'Cold Frosty Morning' was recorded by the Da Costa Woltz Southern Broadcasters in 1927 — one of the earliest Old-Time commercial recordings. Tommy Jarrell (1901–1985), son of fiddler Ben Jarrell, kept this tune alive for generations through his influence at the annual Fiddler's Grove festivals in Union Grove, NC.
tags: tommy jarrell, jam session, G major
notes: Tommy Jarrell learned this from his father Ben Jarrell, who recorded it in 1927. The G major setting sits comfortably in first position — great for beginners but with enough melodic interest to keep advanced players engaged. Play the A part firmly, then let the B part lift slightly. The tune pairs naturally with a banjo in clawhammer style.

title: St. Anne's Reel
description: One of the most widely-played reels in North America, 'St. Anne's Reel' is a point of convergence between Old-Time, Celtic, and Quebec fiddle traditions. Its exact origins are disputed — claimed by both Irish and French-Canadian traditions. It was recorded in the early 20th century by Canadian fiddlers and adopted into Old-Time through the shared dance hall culture of the 19th century.
notes: A deceptively simple tune that rewards clean, even bow strokes. Practice the string crossings in the B part slowly — they can blur at speed if not drilled. This tune crosses genre lines freely: play it in an Old-Time jam, a Celtic session, or a Quebec contradance and you'll fit right in. In Old-Time style, flatten the rhythm slightly; in Celtic style, lift it more.

title: Rye Whiskey
description: A song of whiskey culture from the Appalachian tradition, 'Rye Whiskey' belongs to a broad category of drinking songs that blend humor with genuine pathos. Rye whiskey — distilled from rye grain — was the dominant spirit of the American frontier, produced in home stills throughout Appalachia. The song's modal tonality gives the comedy a darker undertow. It was collected by John Lomax, Cecil Sharp, and multiple folklorists across the Southern mountains.
notes: A song-tune with a wry, world-weary humor — 'Rye whiskey, rye whiskey, rye whiskey I cry / If I don't get rye whiskey I surely will die.' Play it with that resigned, philosophical quality. The modal scale gives it a haunted quality that goes beyond simple comedy. Many fiddlers play it slowly and deliberately, almost like a lament.

title: Cluck Old Hen
description: One of the most peculiarly titled tunes in old-time music, 'Cluck Old Hen' was first transcribed as early as 1886 and recorded most influentially by Fiddlin' John Carson in 1923 — one of the earliest commercial old-time recordings. The tune belongs to the Mixolydian/Dorian modal family that characterizes a large swath of Appalachian music: A Dorian or A Mixolydian depending on the version, with a G natural where a major scale would place a G sharp. The lyrics follow the hen as a rural metaphor: 'My old hen's a good old hen / She lays eggs for the railroad men / Sometimes one and sometimes two / Sometimes enough for the whole damn crew.' The railroad workers, the hen, the counting of eggs — this is the texture of mountain rural life in the late 19th century before electrification, when the railroad was the most powerful external force in every mountain community. Charlie Bowman's version in DGdg tuning and Joe Birchfield's version are among the essential reference recordings. It has been widely played and adapted across Appalachian, bluegrass, and folk revival contexts.
notes: The Mixolydian mode (G natural in an A context) is the tune's soul — if you accidentally play G sharp you lose everything. The melody sits low in the hand, mostly first position, with open-string drones that ring naturally. The lyrical rhythm should drive the bow: 'MY old HEN's a GOOD old HEN' gives you the accent pattern. Try playing it in A Dorian for a darker, bluesier feel that some versions favor. The tune responds well to heavy bow pressure for dancing.

title: Bonaparte's Retreat
description: Named for Napoleon's catastrophic 1812 retreat from Moscow — one of the great military disasters of the 19th century — 'Bonaparte's Retreat' is believed to derive from an older Irish march called 'The Eagle's Whistle' or 'The O'Donovan Clan March.' The tune reached America with Scots-Irish immigrants and was thoroughly naturalized into the Southern fiddle tradition, collecting regional variations from Virginia through Kentucky and Tennessee. The Kentucky version, in A major, became the most widely known through its adoption into the square dance and contradance circuit. Carl Sandburg included a version in 'The American Songbag' (1927), cementing its status as a legitimate American folk artifact. Bill Monroe recorded a definitive version, and it became a standard in the early bluegrass repertoire. The tune's powerful A-part drive and its floating, almost wistful B-part mirror the arc of Napoleon's campaign: confident advance, then disintegration. Bill Harrell's recording and the many versions in the Appalachian fiddle contest tradition are the benchmark references.

title: Liberty
description: Published as early as 1788 in the New York Magazine, 'Liberty' is one of the oldest distinctly American fiddle tunes. Its name reflects the post-Revolutionary spirit, though the tune itself may have older British roots. It became a contest staple across the South and Midwest. Variations abound — some fiddle communities play it in D, others in G.
notes: A tune with enormous rhythmic drive — feel the pulse in your bow arm, not just your fingers. The A part has an ascending run that should build energy. Don't rush; keep a solid floor tempo and let the notes speak. The B part contrast is crucial: the jump up to high position should feel like a release of pressure. Doc Watson and many North Carolina fiddlers favored this one.

title: Black Mountain Rag
description: Doc Watson's arrangement of 'Black Mountain Rag' transformed what was already a well-known piece into one of the defining showpieces of modern old-time and folk guitar. Watson (1923–2012) of Deep Gap, Watauga County, North Carolina, developed his flatpicking technique in relative obscurity before the Newport Folk Festival in 1960 brought him to national attention; 'Black Mountain Rag' became his signature. The tune itself derives from 'Stone's Rag,' a Texas-style fiddle piece by Sidney Stone, which Watson adapted for guitar with dazzling speed and clarity. Black Mountain is a real place — a community in Yancey County, North Carolina — lending the tune its Appalachian identity even as the guitar arrangement drew from the Texas instrumental tradition. For fiddle players, the tune offers a different challenge than for guitarists: the speed and the clean string crossings required to match Watson's clarity at tempo.
notes: This tune is a technical showpiece and should be treated as one. Learn it slowly — the fingering in the B part is treacherous at speed. Doc Watson's recordings are the gold standard; study his phrasing and note choices closely. The A part has a rolling quality; the B part has a leaping, more angular character. Keep the bow close to the bridge for brightness. Don't add ornaments you haven't practiced — at the tempos this tune is usually played, unplanned flourishes become train wrecks.

title: Waterbound
description: In pre-bridge Appalachia, being 'waterbound' — stranded by a flooded creek or river — was a frequent and sometimes dangerous predicament that could last days. Mountain roads followed creek beds and crossed streams repeatedly, making heavy rains an instant barrier. The tune captures the patient waiting of someone stuck on the far bank, watching the water rise and fall. It was widely collected across the Blue Ridge and Smokies.
notes: A song-tune where the 'waterbound' refers to being stranded on the wrong side of a flooded creek — a common predicament in pre-bridge Appalachia. Play it with patient, philosophical energy; being waterbound meant waiting. The melody is gentle and flowing — let the phrases breathe. This is a tune that sounds beautiful played slowly at medium volume.

title: Wildwood Flower
description: Originally published in 1860 as 'I'll Twine 'Mid the Ringlets' by Maud Irving and Joseph Philbrick Webster, the song was transformed by the Carter Family's 1928 Victor recording into the most recognizable guitar piece in American folk music. Sara Carter's rhythm guitar and Maybelle Carter's melody-lead style became the template for country guitar. A.P. Carter adapted the lyrics. The tune's journey from parlor song to country classic exemplifies the Carter Family's role in defining American vernacular music.
tags: carter family, parlor song, singable, history
notes: The fiddle version flows naturally in C major — let the melody sing. This was originally a parlor song ('I'll Twine 'Mid the Ringlets'), and that parlor sensibility should come through: refined, gentle, lyrical. The Carter Family's guitar accompaniment defined the tune's character, but the fiddle version can carry that same dignified quality. Don't rush; let each phrase settle.

title: Chinquapin Hunting
description: The chinquapin (Castanea pumila) is a small native chestnut tree that once grew throughout the Appalachian understory, its sweet nuts harvested by both Native Americans and Appalachian settlers in autumn. Chinquapin hunting — gathering the small, sweet nuts after the first frost — was a beloved seasonal activity for Appalachian children and families. The American chestnut blight (1900–1940) killed billions of trees, including the chinquapin; many communities lost a food source that had fed them for generations. The tune carries an elegiac undertone for a lost landscape.
notes: A light, playful tune — the chinquapin hunt was a children's activity, and the music should have that carefree quality. Keep the bow arm relaxed and the rhythm bouncy. Don't over-articulate; let phrases run together naturally. Works beautifully at a moderate tempo where dancers can actually feel the groove.

title: Fly Around My Pretty Little Miss
description: A song-and-dance tune from the Appalachian tradition, 'Fly Around My Pretty Little Miss' is a courtship song with roots in English and Scots-Irish balladry. The simple verse structure and dancing rhythm made it a social function staple in mountain communities. Collected in multiple versions across Virginia, North Carolina, and Kentucky, it represents the song-tune category — music that exists equally as song and instrumental piece.
notes: A song-tune, meaning the melody follows natural speech rhythm. Sing the words in your head as you play: 'Fly around, my pretty little miss / Fly around, my daisy.' This will help you phrase naturally rather than mechanically. Great for beginners because the form is clear and predictable. Pair it with a banjo for maximum Old-Time effect.

title: Sugar in the Gourd
description: Sugar in the gourd was literally sweet sorghum or cane sugar stored in a dried hollow gourd — a common practice in 19th-century Appalachian households before commercial packaging. Sorghum molasses was one of the few sweeteners available to mountain families. The tune, with its pentatonic leanings and driving rhythm, was collected across multiple Southern states and represents the category of 'household item' tunes that filled the Old-Time repertoire.
notes: A pentatonic-leaning breakdown with a rhythmic hook that hooks listeners immediately. The 'gourd' is a dried hollow gourd used as a water dipper or storage vessel — a staple of 19th-century rural households. Keep the bow arm driving and let the open strings ring. The rhythm has a slight syncopation that's easy to feel once you've found the groove.

title: Wolves A-Howlin
description: Wolves were a genuine presence in Appalachian mountain life well into the 19th century, preying on livestock and occasionally threatening communities. 'Wolves A-Howlin' evokes the frontier soundscape of early settlement — the wild, unpredictable darkness beyond the cabin window. The tune was collected in the Round Peak tradition of Surry County, North Carolina, and is associated with Tommy Jarrell's modal repertoire. The last wolves in Virginia were extirpated around 1900.
tags: tommy jarrell, round peak, modal, howling
notes: One of the most evocative titles in the Old-Time canon — play it like you're hearing wolves in the dark. The modal quality (often Dorian or pentatonic) gives it a genuinely unsettling undertone. Keep the bow slow and heavy in the slower sections. Tommy Jarrell's version is the definitive reference. Don't try to brighten this up — the darkness is the point.

title: Blackest Crow
description: 'Blackest Crow' belongs to the haunted interior of the Appalachian song tradition — a D minor modal song and tune whose lyric confronts the duration of love against the entropy of nature. 'As long as this world will last / I'll love you till the rivers run dry / The blackest crow that ever flew will surely turn to white.' The inversion of natural expectation — the crow turning white, the rivers running dry — defines love as something that will outlast the impossible. The melody is as stark as the lyric: narrow in range, slow in movement, with the kind of simplicity that makes it immediately memorable and devastatingly effective. Multiple versions exist across Virginia, West Virginia, and North Carolina, where it was collected in the early 20th century. Iris DeMent and Tim O'Brien recorded a widely heard version in the folk revival; the tune has also been recorded as a purely instrumental piece.
tags: haunting, minor, D minor, mountain, slow
notes: This is a slow song-tune — don't confuse it with a reel or breakdown. The melody should move at the pace of speech, breathing naturally through each phrase. D minor with a modal quality (watch the 6th and 7th degrees for inflection). Let the longing of the lyric shape your bow arm: long, sustained notes with expressive bow pressure changes. If you learn the words, they'll tell you how to play it. This tune should leave silence in its wake.

title: June Apple
description: Named for a variety of apple that ripens in early summer in the Southern Appalachians, 'June Apple' is a Mixolydian reel with roots in the mountain fiddle tradition. The Mixolydian mode — associated with Scots-Irish modal music — gives it a slightly archaic quality that distinguishes it from major-key dance tunes. It has been collected in multiple versions across Virginia, North Carolina, and Kentucky.

Many players add a slight lilt on the second eighth note of each beat pair for a more authentic Old-Time feel.

title: Leather Britches
description: 'Leather Britches' has one of the most appetizing titles in the old-time repertoire. 'Leather britches' are string beans dried in their pods — a preservation technique widespread across the Appalachian mountains before refrigeration, where the beans were strung on thread and hung to dry in kitchens and porches through late summer, then cooked with fatback through winter. The drying process turns them leathery and chewy, intensifying their flavor. The fiddle tune carrying this name appears in American collections from the 18th century and is almost certainly older still, sharing melodic material with British dance tunes of the same era. It was a ballroom and court dance tune in its earlier life; in the mountains it became a driving reel. Flatpicker Doc Watson recorded an influential version, and it remains one of the most commonly played tunes at Appalachian jams.
tags: ancient, appalachian, G major, folk history
notes: G major with a driving, confident quality that suits its history as a ballroom tune transformed into mountain music. The two parts have distinct characters — A is more rhythmically propulsive, B has a longer melodic line. Doc Watson's flatpicking version gives guitarists a model; fiddle players should match that energy with bow arm weight. The title is a conversation starter: tell the story of dried beans to anyone who asks what 'leather britches' means.

title: New Ground
description: In Southern Appalachian culture, 'new ground' referred to freshly cleared land — forest converted to farmland through the labor-intensive process of felling trees, pulling stumps, and breaking sod. This was one of the defining agricultural experiences of frontier settlement. Tunes named for agricultural activities — 'New Ground,' 'Plowing Under,' 'Harvest Home' — reflect the centrality of farming to rural Southern life and the music that accompanied it.
notes: 'New ground' was the Southern term for land just cleared of trees for the first time — ready for planting. Play this with the energy of clearing that ground: forceful, purposeful, rhythmically driven. The G major setting and open-string drones give it a full, outdoor sound. A natural jam session opener because the form is clear and the rhythm is irresistible.

title: Hickory Jack
description: Hickory (Carya spp.) was one of the most valued trees in the Appalachian forest — hard, shock-resistant, and used for tool handles, wagon wheels, axles, and furniture. The name 'Jack' was a generic working-class name in American folk culture (see also 'Cracker Jack,' 'Flapjack,' 'Steeplejack'). Hickory Jack as a character represents the competent, self-reliant Appalachian worker — the backbone of the mountain economy. The tune has a similar character: reliable, sturdy, unpretentious.
notes: A solid, workmanlike breakdown — 'Hickory Jack' sounds like a character you'd want clearing timber. Play it with honest, grounded energy: no flashy tricks, just clean notes and steady rhythm. The hickory wood reference suggests hardness and durability — bring that quality to the bow arm. Great for session contexts where you want something dependable.

title: Ducks on the Millpond
description: 'Ducks on the Millpond' evokes one of the most pastoral images in Appalachian folk life: the millpond, built to power a grist mill, where the community's grain was ground and where, inevitably, a few ducks would settle on the still water. The millpond was a social hub in mountain communities — a place where neighbors met while waiting for their corn to be ground — and naming a tune for it situates the music in a specific, deeply local world. The tune itself has a gentle, unhurried quality in A major that differs from the driving breakdowns more typical of old-time music, giving it a slightly contemplative character. It was played both as a dance tune and as a piece of pure musical pleasure. The two-part AABB structure is symmetrical and singable.
notes: Let the tune breathe — it's not meant to be driven hard. The A major key with open-string drones gives it a ringing, open quality. Imagine the millpond: still, flat, reflective. The bow should move smoothly rather than driving aggressively. Good for slowing down a jam session or transitioning between faster reels. Play it with the unhurried confidence of someone who isn't in a hurry to get anywhere.

title: Shaking Down the Acorns
description: Mast — the nuts of forest trees including acorns, hickory nuts, beechnuts, and chestnuts — was a critical food source in Appalachian agriculture. Pigs were turned into the forest in autumn to fatten on mast, a practice called pannage or 'masting.' Shaking acorns from low branches and collecting fallen mast was seasonal labor that involved whole families. The tune captures the energetic, festive quality of this autumn harvest activity.
tags: tommy jarrell, round peak, autumn, energetic
notes: A lively, physical tune with a harvest-season energy. Shaking acorns from oak trees was a genuine activity — gathering mast for pigs, making flour, or just for the pleasure of the noise. Keep the rhythm driving and the bow arm active. The tune has a slightly 'falling' quality that reflects the acorns coming down.

title: Granny Does Your Dog Bite
description: A nonsense song-and-dance tune from the Appalachian comic tradition, 'Granny Does Your Dog Bite' belongs to the category of humorous call-and-response pieces that were performed at square dances and play parties. Grandmother figures in Appalachian folk culture were simultaneously respected and gently satirized — their dogs (usually fierce guard dogs on mountain homesteads) were respected too. The tune's light humor reflects the social function of dance music as community entertainment.
notes: A comic question-and-answer song-tune — play it with a grin. The rhythm has a playful hitch to it; don't smooth it out. The humor in the title should come through in the music. Great for children and beginners but satisfying for experienced players who add slurs and ornaments on the repeats.

title: Cricket on the Hearth
description: Named for the beloved hearth cricket of Appalachian mountain homes. The delicate, light bow style needed to render the crickets' chirps makes this a bow technique challenge.
notes: Use a light, fast bow close to the tip — aim for a crisp, chirping sound.

title: Brimstone
description: Brimstone — sulfur — was the scent of hellfire in the fire-and-brimstone preaching tradition of Appalachian evangelical Protestantism. The term appears dozens of times in the King James Bible, always associated with divine wrath and eternal punishment. The tune's dark modal character reflects the theological atmosphere of the Great Awakening revivals and the camp meeting tradition that swept Appalachia from the 1790s onward. Music and religion were inseparable in mountain culture.
notes: A dark, modal tune that earns its hellfire name — brimstone (sulfur) was the smell of hell and damnation in traditional Protestant theology. Don't play this bright or fast; let the modal quality and the darkness develop. A slow-to-medium tempo reveals the menacing character. Let the open strings drone and sustain freely.

title: Log Cabin Blues
description: The log cabin was the defining architectural form of American frontier settlement — built quickly from available timber, warm in winter, intimate in scale. By the early 20th century, the log cabin had become a symbol of hardy American individualism, romanticized in popular culture even as actual log cabins were being replaced by milled-lumber houses. The 'blues' suffix places the tune in the 1920s–1930s commercial folk era when 'blues' attached to traditional tunes signaled a progressive, modern sensibility.
notes: A modal blues tune that lives in a minor-tinged, open-fifth sound world. Don't rush toward the resolution; let the modal ambiguity sit. The log cabin setting suggests isolation, self-sufficiency, and the weight of frontier life. Play it slowly enough that the modal character registers. Good string crossings and clean open-string drones are essential.

title: Nine Hundred Miles
description: A railroad song of uncertain origin that has been collected across multiple American traditions — Appalachian, blues, and labor song. The '900 miles' represents the crushing psychological distance from home experienced by itinerant workers, railroad laborers, and migrants. The Carter Family recorded it; Woody Guthrie recorded it; it appears in Lomax collections. Its wide distribution suggests it was a genuine folk song that traveled with the workers who sang it.
notes: A song-tune about a railroad journey — 'If my woman quits me, Lord, I'm 900 miles from home.' The modal quality gives it genuine pathos. Play slowly and with feeling; don't rush. The melody should feel like the endless monotony of distance. Woody Guthrie and the Carter Family both recorded versions. This is a tune that rewards simplicity over technique.

title: Chinquapin
description: The chinquapin (Castanea pumila) — a small chestnut native to the Appalachian understory — is now rare following the chestnut blight that began in 1900. In earlier centuries it was a food staple, medicine source, and seasonal landmark. This modal tune, distinct from 'Chinquapin Hunting,' uses a minor-pentatonic scale that predates European diatonic harmony — suggesting origins in either very old Scots-Irish tradition or Native American musical contact zones of the Southern Appalachians.
notes: A dark, modal tune — the minor pentatonic scale gives it a haunted, ancient quality. Play slowly and let the open strings drone freely. Don't rush toward the resolution; let the modal ambiguity breathe. Many players find this tune meditative at slow tempos. The chinquapin nut — small, sweet, now mostly gone — gives it an elegiac quality.

title: Bonaparte Crossing the Rhine
description: Napoleon Bonaparte crossed the Rhine River multiple times during his campaigns (1796, 1805, 1813), transforming European political geography. His Rhine crossings were major news events that captured the imagination of ordinary people across the Western world. American fiddle tunes named for Napoleon — 'Bonaparte,' 'Bonaparte's Retreat,' 'Bonaparte Crossing the Rhine' — reflect the intense popular fascination with the French Emperor, who was simultaneously admired for his military genius and feared as a tyrant.
notes: A fast, bright reel with heroic overtones — Napoleon crossing the Rhine was a major historical event, and the tune has that grand, sweeping quality. Keep the bow arm confident and forward. The A part marches; the B part dances. A strong tune for large sessions where you need something with momentum.

title: Old Bunch of Keys
description: A quirky Appalachian reel with a cascading melody that sounds like keys jangling. The unusual title matches the tune's unpredictable character.

title: Hook and Line
description: A D major reel with a fishing theme — the elegant, darting phrases suggest a line cast into a mountain stream.

title: Stoney Creek
description: Stoney Creek is a community in Patrick County, Virginia, in the Blue Ridge foothills near the North Carolina border — one of the richest areas for Old-Time fiddle tradition. The region, associated with the fiddle and banjo style known as Round Peak, produced legendary players including Tommy Jarrell, Fred Cockerham, and Kyle Creed. Water features — creeks, rivers, fords, and springs — were the central landmarks of Appalachian geography, and dozens of tunes carry their names.
tags: henry reed, LOC recording, virginia, grayson county
notes: A cool, clear reel that sounds like the water it's named for. Let the bow float through the phrases with a light, liquid touch. The A part flows downward; the B part rises. Stoney Creek tunes tend to be associated with the Round Peak and Galax regions — play it with that flat-footed, grounded rhythm underneath the flowing melody.

title: Rose Tree
description: An 18th-century English and Irish dance tune, 'Rose Tree' (also 'The Rose Tree') appears in multiple period collections including Playford's Dancing Master tradition. It was one of the tunes that crossed the Atlantic in the early settlement period, carried by British immigrants. The rose was one of the most culturally significant flowers of the European tradition — symbol of love, beauty, and brevity of life. The tune's graceful character reflects its origins in formal social dancing contexts.
notes: A courtly, 18th-century melody with a formal dignity — this tune came from a world of minuets and country dances, not barn dances. Play it with a poised, upright posture in the bow arm and clean, articulate notes. The melodic line has a floral, ornamental quality; let the phrases breathe and complete themselves fully.

title: Lynchburg Town
description: A Virginia reel associated with Lynchburg — a center of trade and culture in the Appalachian mountain region.
tags: virginia, lynchburg, trade town, D major

title: Beaumont Rag
description: 'Beaumont Rag' is among the defining pieces of Texas Western swing and contest fiddle, named for the industrial port city of Beaumont in southeast Texas — oil country, on the Louisiana border, where Cajun and Southern influences merged in a culture distinctly Texan. Bob Wills (1905–1975) and his Texas Playboys popularized the tune and recorded it in the late 1930s; Wills was himself a committed fiddler before becoming primarily a bandleader, and his instrumental recordings document the transformation of old-time fiddle into Western swing. The 'rag' designation signals the syncopation that separates Texas breakdown style from straight old-time: the bow arm must swing, not march. The tune circulates widely at Texas and Southwestern fiddle contests and appears in the repertoires of virtually all serious contest players.
tags: texas swing, bob wills, rag, jazz influence
notes: The syncopation is everything — if you play it straight, you lose the entire point. The bow arm must swing: feel the off-beats, put slight emphasis on the second and fourth eighth notes of each beat pair. Texas style calls for a warm, full tone even at speed; don't let the bow pressure lighten when the tempo rises. The B part has a long, looping melodic line that contrasts with the more rhythmic A part. Listen to Bob Wills's 1930s recordings and study how his fiddlers handled the groove.

title: Salt Creek
description: A reel in the Old-Time tradition that was adopted into early bluegrass by Bill Monroe and popularized through his recordings. 'Salt Creek' — named for a tributary of the White River in Indiana — represents the crossover moment when Old-Time fiddle material entered the nascent bluegrass vocabulary. The tune's popularity on both sides of the genre divide makes it a useful bridge for musicians crossing between communities.
notes: A tune that lives at the boundary of Old-Time and bluegrass — Bill Monroe played it, which elevated its profile enormously. The bow arm needs to be relaxed but powerful; the 8th notes should flow like a stream. The B part is the technical challenge: those descending runs need to be drilled slowly before building speed. Clean left-hand articulation is key.

title: Grey Eagle
description: An A major breakdown with deep Texas contest fiddle roots, 'Grey Eagle' appears in early fiddle contest records from the 1880s and was collected by Marion Thede in her 1967 compendium 'The Fiddle Book.' The eagle — symbol of American independence — gave the tune its proud, bright character. It was a showpiece for demonstrating high-position technique and clean string crossings at Southern fiddling contests.
