Keep the A part grounded with strong downbows, then lift for the B part. This tune rewards confident playing; timid bowing makes it sound thin.

title: Dusty Miller
description: A tune of Scottish and Irish origin, 'Dusty Miller' references the miller whose clothes were perpetually covered in flour dust — a stock figure in British folk humor and song. Published in multiple early collections including Gow's 'Repository of the Dance Music of Scotland' (1799), it crossed the Atlantic and appeared in American fiddle books throughout the 19th century. The name was applied to various tunes across traditions, suggesting it functioned as a generic 'miller's tune.'
notes: An old tune with a courtly feel — don't rush it. The dotted rhythms in some versions suggest a mild hornpipe influence. The A part has a satisfying arc that should feel inevitable; the B part offers contrast. In Scottish tradition this is played with more ornamentation; in Old-Time settings it's typically stripped down and driven forward.

title: Over the Waterfall
description: A reel of unclear origin that has circulated widely across Old-Time, Cajun, and Celtic traditions. Its neutral melodic character — pleasant but not highly distinctive — may explain its adaptability across styles. It has been published in both American fiddle collections and Irish music compendia. The name evokes a natural image that fits the smooth, flowing melody.
notes: The key to this tune is perfectly even 8th notes — no swinging, no rushing. Let the bow flow smoothly across strings with minimal pressure. The D major setting means all four open strings are available as drones. Great for practicing smooth string crossings. In Cajun settings, this tune gets a very different treatment — slicker and more ornamental.

title: Brilliancy
description: 'Brilliancy' is a demanding Texas contest fiddle piece whose name announces its purpose: this is music designed to dazzle. Contest fiddling in the South and Southwest developed a distinct performance culture in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, with competitors expected to showcase technical facility — high-position playing, rapid string crossings, ornamental variations — alongside musical taste. 'Brilliancy' belongs to this category of purposeful showpieces, where the melody is a vehicle for demonstrating what a fiddler can do. The tune appears in Texas fiddle contest culture by the early 20th century and was circulated by contest veterans who passed it to younger players as a teaching piece for advanced technique.
notes: The name is a challenge. 'Brilliancy' expects you to be brilliant — clear tone, clean articulation, high-position comfort, and confident tempo. Learn it slowly and build speed only after every note is clean. The high-register passages are the technical core: bow pressure must stay consistent even as the bow works near the tip. Contest players usually learn multiple variations; if you know only the base melody, it doesn't yet dazzle. Keep working.

title: Bob Wills Breakdown
description: Bob Wills (1905–1975), the 'King of Western Swing,' was born in Limestone County, Texas into a deep fiddle family. His father and grandfather were both contest fiddlers. Wills merged Old-Time Texas fiddle with jazz harmonies, jazz horns, and a dancehall groove to create Western swing in the 1930s. His band, the Texas Playboys, recorded prolifically for Columbia and Vocalion. Bob Wills was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 1968.
tags: bob wills, western swing, jazz, dancehall
notes: This tune captures the essence of Western swing — a groove that floats between Old-Time fiddle drive and jazz swing feel. Don't play it dead straight; let the bow breathe slightly on the offbeats. Bob Wills' rhythm was infectious — he drove his band from the back of the stage, hollering encouragement while playing. Find that same looseness.

title: Lee Highway Blues
description: US Route 11 — designated 'Lee Highway' after Confederate General Robert E. Lee — was one of the first numbered US highways (1926), running from Washington DC through the Shenandoah Valley and down through Tennessee and Alabama. It was a major route before Interstate 81 supplanted it. The highway blues tradition reflects Depression-era experience of migration, displacement, and the search for work along American roads.
tags: bob wills, blues, swing, texas playboys
notes: A tune with a 1930s highway feel — somewhere between a breakdown and a blues. The 'blues' quality comes from the bent notes and slight drag on certain beats. Don't play it too clean; let some rawness through. US Route 11 (Lee Highway) cuts through Virginia and Tennessee — play this like you're driving it late at night.

title: Faded Love
description: 'Faded Love' was written by Bob Wills (1905–1975) and his father, John Tompkins Wills, who had played an older fiddle tune that Bob adapted into the version recorded by the Texas Playboys in 1950. The song's lyric — about a love that has faded like the roses in the rain — became one of the great country love songs, recorded by Patsy Cline in 1963 in a version that reached millions of listeners who had never heard of Bob Wills. The melody has a quality rare in fiddle music: it's equally effective as an instrumental, a slow country ballad, and a dance waltz, because the tune itself carries emotional weight that doesn't depend on lyrics. The chord progression moves through the circle of fifths in a way that sounds both inevitable and surprising, giving trained musicians something to admire alongside the accessible beauty that non-musicians simply feel.
tags: bob wills, western swing, waltz, patsy cline, country classic
notes: A waltz in G major, played slowly and with feeling. The bow arm should be relaxed and the tone warm — this is not the place for a bright, driving stroke. The melody rises and falls in long arcs; follow those arcs with your bow and don't interrupt them for ornament. Patsy Cline's 1963 recording is the vocal benchmark. For instrumental versions, listen to the Texas Playboys original. The final phrase should leave the room quiet for a moment.

title: Dallas Rag
description: Dallas, Texas was a major center of commercial country and western music recording in the 1920s and 1930s. Labels including Columbia, Victor, and OKeh regularly staged recording sessions in Dallas to capture the rich musical culture of the Southwest — from Western swing to gospel to string band music. 'Dallas Rag' evokes this era of commercial folk recording when the city was a crossroads of African American, white Southern, and Mexican musical traditions.
notes: A 1920s ragtime-inflected tune with syncopation that should feel natural, not forced. The 'rag' quality comes from the rhythmic displacement — lean into the off-beats. This sits in the same sonic territory as 'Peacock Rag' and 'Dallas Rag' recordings from the early commercial era. Let the bow arm swing slightly.

title: Midnight on the Water
description: 'Midnight on the Water' is widely attributed to Luke Thomasson and/or Charles Cunningham of Bosque County, Texas, and is one of the most hauntingly beautiful tunes in the American fiddle tradition. The D minor waltz has a quality of still, dark water — which is precisely what the title evokes — and in the right hands can stop a crowded dance hall. Texas fiddler Benny Thomasson (Luke's son) made it a centerpiece of his contest performances, and the tune spread through the contest circuit into wider circulation. It belongs to a category of Texas fiddle waltzes — along with 'Over the Waterfall' and 'Over the Waves' — that function more as slow, expressive performance pieces than as functional dance accompaniment. The three-part structure (AABBCC) gives it more room to develop than a standard two-part tune.
notes: Play this alone, in the dark, for someone you love. D minor with a plaintive, singing melody that asks for a long, slow bow and maximum tone. Don't rush any phrase — this is one of the few fiddle tunes where slowing down only improves it. The high point of the C part should be the emotional peak of the performance; build toward it in the A and B parts. Benny Thomasson's recordings are the essential reference. This is the tune that makes non-musicians understand what a fiddle can do.

title: Yellow Rose of Texas
description: 'The Yellow Rose of Texas' was first published in 1853, attributed to 'J.K.,' and is believed to reference Emily D. West, a free Black woman from New York who may have distracted General Santa Anna during the Battle of San Jacinto in 1836. The tune became Texas's unofficial anthem and was a Civil War marching song for Confederate troops. Mitch Miller's 1955 recording sold over a million copies, cementing its place in American popular memory.
notes: Play it bright and forward — this is a marching tune at heart. The bow should feel light and lifted, not heavy and pressed. The simple four-bar structure repeats enough to allow variation: add slides on the repeats, or ornament the long notes. Great for building a steady, reliable tempo. Audiences always recognize it, which gives you confidence.

title: Peacock Rag
description: The ragtime influence on Old-Time fiddling was substantial in the 1920s — Scott Joplin's rags (1899–1917) had permeated popular culture, and fiddle players absorbed the syncopated rhythms into their repertoire. 'Peacock Rag' belongs to a category of rag-influenced dance tunes that appeared in Southern and Midwestern fiddle contests of the 1920s, reflecting the era's appetite for modern, syncopated music. The peacock's flamboyant display suggested the showmanship required.
notes: A 1920s rag-influenced tune with a strut to it — a peacock spreads its tail to show off, and you should bring some of that pride to the playing. The syncopation should feel natural and hip, not mechanical. This is a tune where tone quality matters: a full, warm sound in the upper strings makes the showoff quality land.

title: Texas Gales
description: A Texas reel with a rushing, wind-swept quality. The wide intervallic leaps and fast bow strokes suggest the open prairie in a strong wind.

title: Hull's Victory
description: Written to celebrate Captain Isaac Hull's naval victory over HMS Guerriere in 1812. A stately hornpipe with dotted rhythms evoking military fanfares.
notes: Play with a strong, dotted hornpipe rhythm — not too fast. Feel the military pride.

title: Flowers of Edinburgh
description: A Scottish reel from the 18th century, 'Flowers of Edinburgh' appears in Robert Bremner's 'Collection of Scots Reels' (c.1757) and later in Nathaniel Gow's publications. It crossed the Atlantic and became a fixture of New England contradance tradition, appearing in early American dance manuals. The Edinburgh reference evokes the cosmopolitan culture of Scotland's capital during its Enlightenment period.
notes: One of the most elegant reels in the Anglo-American tradition. The stately feel should come through even at speed — this is not a rough-edged breakdown. Play with a smooth, sustained bow stroke and let the phrases breathe. The B part has a particularly beautiful descending line. In contra dance settings, this tune can carry enormous energy without losing its refinement.

title: Rakes of Mallow
description: An Irish reel named for the town of Mallow, County Cork, 'Rakes of Mallow' was published in O'Neill's collections and carried across the Atlantic by Irish immigrants. 'Rakes' — young men who lived for pleasure and dissipation — were stock characters of 18th-century Irish folk humor. The tune settled into New England contradance tradition and remains a staple of sessions on both sides of the Atlantic.
tags: irish origin, contra dance, bouncy, beginner
notes: A bouncy G major reel with great forward drive. 'Rakes' in the title refers to dissolute men about town — the tune has a mischievous, light-footed character. Keep the bow near the tip for lightness in the A part. The B part has a longer sustained feel. This tune works beautifully for contradancing and was a staple of American dance halls in the 19th century.

title: Money Musk
description: 'Money Musk' is one of the oldest and most historically documented reels in the New England and American fiddle tradition. It appears in print as early as 1788 in William Vickers's Scottish dance book, under the name 'My Lord Musk's Reel' — Lord Musk being a Scottish nobleman whose estate name lent the tune its label before American corruption turned it into 'Money Musk.' The tune crossed the Atlantic with Scots-Irish and English immigrants and became foundational in New England contradance music; it appears in virtually every early American dance manual and fiddle collection, including Ryan's Mammoth Collection (1883). It was played at community dances for over two centuries in the same communities, making it a living thread connecting the colonial era to the present. The straightforward D major reel structure — clear 8-bar strains, symmetrical phrasing — is ideal for contradancing with large numbers of couples.
notes: D major with a formal, stately quality that reflects its Scottish courtly origins. Play it with precision and flow: clean string crossings, even 8th notes, no rushing. New England style calls for less ornament than Irish style but more drive than the parlor version. This tune has been played continuously for over 200 years in New England — treat it with appropriate respect. Good for contra dance callers because the phrases are mathematically even and the melody is memorable after one hearing.

title: Glise a Sherbrooke
description: Sherbrooke is a city in the Eastern Townships of Quebec, a region settled by both French Canadians and English-speaking Loyalists after the American Revolution. The French-Canadian fiddle tradition — driven by Catholic social culture, parish dances, and a rich repertoire of reels, jigs, and hornpipes — is one of the oldest continuous fiddle traditions in North America. Quebec fiddlers like Joseph Allard and Jean Carignan developed a highly ornamented, technically demanding style that influenced players throughout the Northeast.
notes: A French-Canadian reel with a distinctive gliding character — 'glise' means 'glide' or 'slide' in French. The bowing should emphasize smooth connections between notes, with strategic slurs that give it a flowing quality. This is a tune where the phrasing matters as much as the notes. Quebec fiddlers play it with a characteristic lilt that Old-Time players often approximate.

title: Lady of the Lake
description: Inspired by Sir Walter Scott's enormously popular 1810 epic poem 'The Lady of the Lake,' set in the Scottish Highlands, this waltz rode the wave of Romantic-era Scottish cultural enthusiasm that swept both Britain and America in the early 19th century. Scott's poem was so influential that it sparked a tourism boom in the Scottish Highlands and influenced countless folk tunes, songs, and dances named for its characters. The tune circulated in parlor music collections throughout the 19th century.
notes: A graceful, aristocratic waltz — the bow should float, never dig. The 3/4 rhythm should feel like breathing, not counting. Let the phrases arc up and back down. This tune rewards a slow tempo and a long, smooth bow. It's a formal dance piece from the parlor tradition; bring some courtliness to it.

title: Fisher's Hornpipe
description: Composed by Johann Fischer (c.1733–1800), a German-born musician who settled in London, 'Fisher's Hornpipe' was published around 1780. It crossed the Atlantic and was embraced in New England contradance and Southern fiddle traditions alike. The hornpipe style — originally a sailor's dance — features characteristic dotted rhythms that distinguish it from reels. Thompson's 'Compleat Collection of 200 Favourite Country Dances' preserves early versions.
tags: hornpipe, dotted rhythm, english origin, widespread
notes: The defining feature of hornpipe style is the dotted rhythm — long-short, long-short. Don't rush the dots; hornpipes should feel stately, not scrambled. Fisher's has an elegance that rewards clean bow changes. The B part has a descending run that should flow smoothly. Many fiddlers add a slight pause at phrase endings in traditional style.

title: Temperance Reel
description: The American temperance movement of the 19th century was one of the most powerful social reform campaigns in US history, culminating in Prohibition (1920–1933). Temperance groups often used popular fiddle tunes at their meetings to draw crowds, renaming them with morally improving titles. 'Temperance Reel' is one of several tunes that acquired teetotaling associations while remaining stubbornly associated with dancing and festivity.
notes: A tune whose name was borrowed by the temperance movement for anti-alcohol campaigns — play it with cheerful defiance. The reel is bright and quick, with a clear two-part structure. Keep the bow light and let the phrases bounce. Despite its abstemious name, this tune has always sounded better at a dance where someone has brought a jug.

title: New Five Cents
description: The 'new five cents' likely refers to the Buffalo nickel (Indian Head nickel), introduced in 1913, which replaced the Liberty Head design and became immediately popular for its artistic merit. The coin featured a Native American portrait on the obverse and an American buffalo (bison) on the reverse, designed by sculptor James Earle Fraser. In folk music, naming tunes for currency ('Two Bits,' 'Dollar Tune') was a common device suggesting either the tune's value or its association with pay-day celebrations.
tags: contra dance, new england, bright, clean
notes: A reel with the jaunty confidence of new money — the 1913 nickel (the Buffalo nickel) was a point of national pride. Keep the rhythm bright and forward-moving. The two-part structure is clear and well-defined; don't blur the seam between A and B. A good tune for building speed at jam sessions because the form is predictable.

title: Rocky Road to Dublin
description: A rousing Irish jig in E minor that became popular in New England dance tradition. The 6/8 rhythm is a welcome change of pace from the usual 4/4 breakdowns.
tags: jig, irish origin, em minor, 6/8, dance
notes: The jig feel is fundamentally different from breakdowns — learn to internalize the 6/8 pulse.

title: Drowsy Maggie
description: An Irish reel that crossed the Atlantic and became naturalized in New England contradance music, 'Drowsy Maggie' was printed in O'Neill's 'The Dance Music of Ireland' (1907). Its name likely refers to a fictional sleepy girl — a common trope in Irish naming conventions. The tune's E minor tonality is unusual enough to make it stand out in any session, contributing to its widespread adoption across traditions.
tags: irish origin, em minor, contra dance, new england
notes: The E minor key gives this tune a darker, more introspective quality than most reels. Let the minor color show — don't rush toward brightness. The B part lifts slightly before resolving back to E minor. In Celtic style, ornament with cuts and rolls; in Old-Time style, keep it smoother with more bow drive. Works beautifully at contradance speed.

title: Paddy on the Turnpike
description: The 'turnpike' was the 19th century's principal form of improved road — a toll road, often plank or macadamized, that allowed faster travel than muddy forest tracks. 'Paddy' — the stock Irish immigrant character — walking the turnpike represented the experience of the massive Irish immigration of the 1840s–1860s. Irish laborers built many of the turnpikes, canals, and railroads they appear in. The tune blends Irish reel structure with American square dance energy.
tags: irish immigrant, contra dance, new england, history
notes: An Irish-American reel with a driving, forward energy — 'Paddy' is going somewhere and doesn't plan to stop. Keep the bow arm pushing through phrases. The turnpike setting suggests purposeful travel. This tune sits at the crossroads of Irish and Appalachian styles; either approach works, though the Old-Time version tends to iron out some of the Irish ornaments.

title: Cotton-Eyed Joe
description: One of the most geographically widespread tunes in American folk music, 'Cotton-Eyed Joe' appears in both pre-Civil War minstrelsy and post-war Southern fiddle traditions. The lyrics reference an itinerant worker with eye disease. John A. Lomax collected it in Texas in the 1930s. The tune diverged into regional styles: a driving Appalachian version and a more elaborate Texas contest version.
notes: The Texas contest version is much faster and more ornamented than the Appalachian version — know which one your jam group plays. The A part uses a repetitive hook that makes it easy to learn but hard to play with real drive. Keep the drone strings ringing and accent the offbeats lightly. In Texas style, add quick slides into notes.

title: Mississippi Sawyer
description: 'Mississippi Sawyer' was first documented in print in the 1880s but is certainly older. The sawyer — a submerged log that bobs up and down in a river current — was one of the greatest hazards of 19th-century river navigation. Mark Twain described their dangers on the Mississippi. The tune's powerful, forward-driving character seems to capture the rhythm of a great river. It appears in multiple Southern fiddle collections.
notes: A powerful tune with a confident, striding melody. The 'sawyer' was a floating log — or a cluster of logs — on the Mississippi that could sink a steamboat without warning. Channel that unpredictability: keep the drive steady but let phrase endings snap. The B part has a particularly strong close. This tune works beautifully at outdoor sessions and contradances.

title: Bile Them Cabbage Down
description: 'Bile Them Cabbage Down' has been teaching new fiddlers to hold a bow for well over a century. The title refers to boiling (or 'biling' in Appalachian dialect) cabbage — a dietary staple of mountain households through autumn and winter. The tune appears in Southern collections from the 19th century and was played at community gatherings as both dance music and an informal teaching tool, since the two-part pentatonic structure in D major is almost entirely playable in first position with no complex string crossings. Its famous lyrics — 'Bile them cabbage down, boys / Bake them hoe-cakes brown / The only song that I can sing is bile them cabbage down' — exemplify the functional simplicity of mountain social song, where the text exists to give the room something to sing while the fiddler drives the dance.
notes: Start every new student on this tune. D major, first position, no fancy stuff. The bow should move evenly from frog to tip on the long notes; the short notes should be crisp. Singing the words while playing teaches phrasing more effectively than any metronome. For more advanced players, try adding open-string drones under the melody and see how many double-stops you can work in without losing the flow. This is also a perfect singing lesson tune.

title: Red Haired Boy
description: Known in Ireland as 'The Little Beggarman,' this Mixolydian reel was carried to America by Irish immigrants in the 18th century and embedded itself deeply in Appalachian and Southern fiddle traditions. The lowered 7th gives it a modal quality that distinguishes it from major-key reels. It appears in O'Neill's 'Music of Ireland' (1903) and has been collected across Appalachia under dozens of names.
notes: The Mixolydian mode (natural 7th scale degree flattened) is the key to this tune's character — lean into that G-natural in an A context. Don't accidentally sharpen it into G#. The tune sits in first position throughout and works beautifully at moderate speed. In Southern Old-Time style, keep the bow smooth and singing; in Appalachian style, add more drive and grit.

title: Sourwood Mountain
description: Named for the Sourwood tree (Oxydendrum arboreum), a native Appalachian tree prized for its honey and autumn color, 'Sourwood Mountain' is one of the most widely-collected Old-Time songs. Cecil Sharp documented it in his 'English Folk Songs from the Southern Appalachians' (1917), noting its popularity across western North Carolina and Virginia. The sourwood's late-summer blooming — when mountain bees produce distinctive sourwood honey — marked a seasonal moment in the Appalachian agricultural calendar.
notes: A song-tune with a strong, singable hook. 'Chickens a-crowing on Sourwood Mountain, hey-ho-dee-dee-dee.' Keep the rhythm lively and the melody bright — this is a courting song with a good-natured energy. The A major setting gives it warmth. Many players add open-string drones on the long notes. Great for contradances and social gatherings.

title: Cumberland Gap
description: Cumberland Gap — the natural passage through the Cumberland Mountains at the convergence of Virginia, Kentucky, and Tennessee — was the gateway for hundreds of thousands of settlers pushing west through the Appalachians in the late 18th century. Daniel Boone blazed the Wilderness Road through it in 1775. The tune, named for this frontier passage, became a symbol of westward expansion and was collected widely across the South.
notes: A natural first tune for beginners — simple structure, open-string drones, and a memorable hook. Keep the bow arm relaxed and let the open strings ring between notes. The tune sounds great at moderate speed with hard downbows on beat one. Once comfortable, try adding a drone note below the melody on the repeat.

title: Hawk's Got a Chicken
description: Chicken hawks (red-tailed hawks, Cooper's hawks) were a genuine menace to Appalachian farmsteads, regularly taking chickens from the yard in the sudden, devastating strike that gave this tune its name. Farmers went to considerable lengths to protect their flocks. In the folk imagination, the hawk became a symbol of sudden loss and the unpredictability of rural life. Animal-hunt tunes — 'Fox Chase,' 'Hawk's Got a Chicken,' 'Cat's Got the Measles' — formed a whole genre of narrative fiddle music.
notes: A dramatic, predator-energy tune — the hawk's strike should be felt in the rhythm. Keep the bow arm sharp and decisive. The syncopated rhythm suggests the sudden, violent swoop of a hawk on unsuspecting poultry. This is a great uptempo showstopper. Don't smooth out the edges; the roughness is part of the character.

title: Cackling Hen
description: An imitative tune that mimics the sounds of a cackling hen. A favorite for trick fiddlers and a demonstration of how Old-Time music imitates rural farm life.
tags: imitative, trick fiddling, farm life, humorous
notes: The staccato ornaments imitate clucking — play them bright and short.

title: Golden Slippers
description: Written by James A. Bland (1854–1911), one of the most successful African American songwriters of the 19th century, 'Oh Dem Golden Slippers' (1879) sold over 100,000 sheet music copies within a year of publication. Bland wrote over 700 songs, including 'Carry Me Back to Old Virginny.' The fiddle tune version stripped the song to its essence and became a parade and dance hall standard across the American South.
notes: The minstrel origins of this tune don't change the fact that it swings beautifully. Play it with a light, buoyant bow — don't dig in. The verse and chorus have different feels; the chorus lifts. This tune adapted naturally into the fiddle tradition because the melody is so strong. Listen to early recordings to hear the swagger it carries.

title: Ida Red
description: 'Ida Red' is one of the most historically consequential tunes in American music — Chuck Berry acknowledged it as a primary inspiration for 'Maybellene' (1955), his debut hit that effectively invented rock and roll's guitar vocabulary. The fiddle tune itself dates from at least the 1930s and was recorded by Bob Wills and His Texas Playboys among many others; Wills's versions helped establish the 'Ida Red' groove as a Western swing staple. Earlier still, the tune appears in the oral tradition as a Southern breakdown, with a repetitive, circular melody that creates a driving, hypnotic rhythm especially effective at the medium-fast tempos typical of dance music. That same quality — the relentless forward pull of a melody that never quite resolves — made it a perfect foundation for Chuck Berry to build rock and roll on.
notes: The groove is everything. Find a tempo that feels inevitable — not rushed, not dragged — and lock into it. The melody almost loops back on itself; that circularity is intentional and creates the hypnotic quality that made this tune a rock and roll blueprint. A major with open-string drones. Keep the bow pressure steady and resist the urge to add too much ornament; the power of this tune is in its relentlessness. Play it until the groove finds you.

title: Ragtime Annie
description: A fiddle tune that absorbed the ragtime craze of the early 20th century, 'Ragtime Annie' blends the older Southern reel tradition with the syncopated rhythms of 1900s popular music. The tune represents the constant dialogue between folk fiddling and commercial music — a two-way street that shaped American music throughout the 20th century. It has been recorded by artists across Old-Time, bluegrass, and Western swing traditions.
notes: The ragtime influence is in the syncopation — feel the offbeat accents in the A part without forcing them. This should swing, not march. The B part is more straightforward, providing rhythmic contrast. Many players add a slight drag on the syncopated notes to emphasize the ragtime feel. Listen to early 1920s recordings to hear how fiddlers absorbed the era's popular music.

title: Georgia Railroad
description: The Western & Atlantic Railroad (the 'Georgia Railroad' line) was built between 1836 and 1851, connecting Atlanta to Chattanooga and opening up the interior South to commerce. The Great Locomotive Chase of 1862, in which Union spies stole a Confederate train on this line, became one of the Civil War's most dramatic episodes. The tune captures the rhythmic excitement of the railroad age — one of the defining technological experiences of 19th-century American life.
notes: A late 19th-century tune with a locomotive feel — keep the rhythm absolutely steady, like a train on rails. The A part has a call-and-response structure; the B part is more melodic. This works well at sessions when you want to establish a solid tempo reference for the group. Don't rush the tempo; a locomotive moves at a constant speed.

title: Tennessee Wagoner
description: 'Tennessee Wagoner' first appeared in print in the late 19th century but is certainly older, referencing the wagoning trade — freight transport by horse-drawn wagon — that was central to Appalachian commerce before railroads. Wagoners were significant cultural figures: independent, hard-living, often musical. The tune's relentless forward drive captures the rhythm of a loaded wagon on a mountain road.
tags: driving, A major, bow technique, historical
notes: This tune has a confident, roadhouse swagger. The A part should feel inevitable — each phrase arrives like a wheel hitting a rut in the road. The B part offers rhythmic variation. Named for the wagoners who drove freight over Tennessee mountain passes, the tune's steady drive evokes long hauls and hard work. Keep the tempo rock-solid; this is not a tune for fluctuating tempos.

title: Billy in the Lowground
description: 'Billy in the Lowground' is among the most beloved C major tunes in the old-time tradition, with a name that places it in the landscape of the Southern lowlands — the 'lowground,' a low-lying field near a creek or river, often marshy, often the best agricultural land in a mountainous region. The tune is widely collected across the Appalachian mountains and has multiple variants across Virginia, North Carolina, Tennessee, and Kentucky. The name 'Billy' likely refers to a specific person known in the community where the tune was named — a common naming practice in the oral tradition — though no historical Billy has been definitively identified. The C major key is relatively rare in old-time fiddle music; most tunes favor G, D, or A, so 'Billy in the Lowground' stands out in any session for its distinctive harmonic color. The tune has been recorded by many artists including the New Lost City Ramblers.
tags: C major, uncommon key, beloved, warm
notes: The C major key gives this tune a warm, slightly darker quality than the brighter D and A keys. The first finger plays C and F throughout, which requires good intonation attention. The two-part structure is symmetrical and the melody has a natural lilt that rewards a slight swing. Good for practicing intonation in a less familiar key. Don't rush the descending phrase at the end of the A part — that moment is the tune's emotional center.

title: Sitting on Top of the World
description: First recorded by the Mississippi Sheiks (Walter Vinson and Lonnie Chatmon) in 1930 for Okeh Records, 'Sitting on Top of the World' became one of the most-covered songs in American music — recorded by Bob Wills, Doc Watson, Howlin Wolf, the Grateful Dead, Eric Clapton, and dozens of others. The Mississippi Sheiks were a Black string band from Jackson, Mississippi who moved fluidly between blues, Old-Time, and pop styles, reflecting the integrated musical world of the early recording era.
notes: A blues-influenced breakdown from the 1920s — the syncopation is essential. Don't play this straight; the rhythm needs to breathe and swing slightly. The lyrical version ('Was in the spring, one summer's day / When my good gal left me, she left me to stay') should be in your ear. A tune that lives at the crossroads of blues and country.

title: Liza Jane
description: One of the most widely-distributed African American song-and-dance tunes, 'Little Liza Jane' appears in print from the 1880s but is certainly older. Collected by John and Alan Lomax in multiple Southern states, the song was associated with ring plays, work songs, and dance music in Black communities. It crossed into the white fiddle tradition through the shared musical culture of the rural South and became a standard of both Old-Time and early bluegrass music.
notes: A classic song-tune — sing 'Little Liza Jane' in your head as you play. The melody has a natural lift and bounce that should carry through the bow. Keep the rhythm slightly syncopated in the A part for maximum groove. This is a tune that wants to be played loud and with confidence. Great opener for a jam — simple enough for beginners, satisfying for advanced players.

title: Old Sledge
description: Old Sledge (also called Seven Up, High-Low-Jack, or All Fours) was the dominant card game of colonial and early American society, played in taverns, on riverboats, and at social gatherings throughout the South and West. The game, brought from England in the 17th century, was widely played by all social classes. Games named for cards and gambling — 'Old Sledge,' 'Poker Night,' 'Faro' — reflect the central role of social gaming in pre-radio rural entertainment culture.
tags: card game, history, G major, driving
notes: A breakdown named for a card game — 'Seven Up' or 'Old Sledge' was the most popular American card game from the 1600s through the mid-19th century. Play with the quick, decisive energy of a card player laying down a winning hand. The rhythm should be sharp and articulate, not smooth. Good tune for demonstrating clean string crossings.

title: Whiskey in the Jar
description: One of the oldest surviving Irish folk songs, 'Whiskey in the Jar' tells the story of an Irish highwayman betrayed by his lover. Versions appear in print from the early 18th century. It was carried to America by Irish immigrants and naturalized in the Southern mountain tradition. Metallica's 1998 cover introduced it to a new generation, but the tune's roots are firmly in 300 years of Irish oral tradition.
notes: A song-tune — let the words guide the phrasing: 'As I was going over the far-famous Kerry mountains...' The melody should breathe naturally, not march. The G major key and simple structure make this accessible for beginners, but the singing quality takes time to develop. Many fiddlers ornament the long notes with gentle vibrato or a bow accent.

title: Sweet Sunny South
description: A song of post-Civil War Southern nostalgia, 'Sweet Sunny South' was written in the 1850s and achieved enormous popularity after the Civil War as a vehicle for Lost Cause sentiment. Henry Reed's LOC recording (afcreed000154) captures a Virginia fiddler's version that strips it to its essential melody. The 'Sunny South' was a complex cultural symbol — representing both genuine homesickness and the idealization of an antebellum past that obscured its brutalities.
tags: waltz, civil war, parlor, nostalgic, slow
notes: A Southern waltz with genuine tenderness — play it with a long, sustained bow and real feeling. The 'Sweet Sunny South' was a nostalgia trope in post-Civil War Southern culture: a longing for a pre-war life that was partly real, partly mythologized. Let that bittersweet quality come through. Three-quarter time should feel like breathing.

title: Aragon Mill
description: A haunting D minor tune about a textile mill closing in Aragon, Georgia. One of the great labor songs of the New Lost City Ramblers era.
tags: labor song, mill town, haunting, georgia, new lost city ramblers
notes: Play this with weight and sadness — it's a mourning song for a lost community.

title: Whoa Mule
description: Mule humor was a staple of Southern folk culture — the animal's stubbornness, strength, and occasional unpredictability made it a natural comic subject. 'Whoa Mule' joins 'Flop-Eared Mule,' 'Kicking Mule,' and 'Goodbye Old Paint' in the category of working-animal tunes that celebrated the central role of draft animals in pre-mechanized Southern agriculture. The mule (a hybrid of horse and donkey) was preferred over horses for farm work in the South because of its endurance and disease resistance.
notes: A comic, mule-themed breakdown with an insistent energy — the mule won't stop, and neither should the fiddler. Keep the tempo steady and the bow arm driving. The humor comes from the relentless forward motion that mirrors the tune's subject. A good session opener when you want to set a strong, clear tempo.

title: Blue Railroad Train
description: Railroad tunes were among the most popular genres in early commercial country music — the train was the defining technology of the era, connecting isolated communities to the wider world and carrying both hope and heartbreak. 'Blue Railroad Train' reflects the early 20th-century recording industry's fascination with train imagery, which appeared in hundreds of songs from the Carter Family, Jimmy Rodgers, and countless regional artists.
notes: A train tune — keep the rhythm as steady as a locomotive. The 'blue' in the title suggests a mournful quality beneath the driving rhythm. Don't rush; a train moves at a constant, powerful pace. The breakdown character suits both contest playing and informal session settings. Listen for the rhythmic 'chug' underneath the melody.

title: Kitchen Breakdown
description: A Southern kitchen dance tune — the melody has a cheerful, domestic quality suggesting informal dancing in front of a wood stove.

title: Big Sandy River
description: Named for the Big Sandy River that forms the border between Kentucky and West Virginia, this reel captures the rolling landscape of the region. The Big Sandy watershed was heavily settled by Scots-Irish families in the late 18th century who brought their fiddle traditions with them. The tune's smooth, rolling character evokes the river itself — wide, steady, and deep.
notes: A rolling, river-smooth reel — let the bow float through the phrases without digging in. The G major key with open strings available as drones gives it a full, resonant sound. Keep the tempo steady; this tune's character comes from evenness, not excitement. At Midwest fiddle contests it's often played with a slightly more swinging feel than Appalachian style.

title: Hog-Eyed Man
description: A sailor's song of the mid-19th century that made its way from American seaports into the inland fiddle tradition, 'Hog-Eyed Man' (also 'Hog Eye') was sung on sailing ships and collected by folklorist Carl Sandburg in 'The American Songbag' (1927). The 'hog-eyed man' — a rough, working sailor — represents the world of maritime labor culture. The tune's migration from sea to mountain demonstrates how American folk music traveled along trade routes.
notes: A song-tune with a comic, earthy character. Let the words guide the phrasing: 'A hog-eyed man is the man for me, hog-eyed man of Tennessee.' The humor should come through in the rhythm. Keep the bow light and bouncy in the A part. This was a sailor's song originally — play it with a rollicking, shipboard swagger.

title: Lost Indian
description: Recorded by Henry Reed of Glen Lyn, Virginia for the Library of Congress in 1966, 'Lost Indian' is a modal pentatonic tune with an ancient quality that suggests Native American or very early Scots-Irish influence. The name evokes the contact zone between European settlers and Native American peoples in the Appalachian frontier. Similar tunes appear in both Cherokee and Scots-Irish traditions, raising questions about cultural exchange that musicologists continue to investigate.
notes: One of the great modal tunes — the pentatonic scale and open, spacious phrases give it a genuinely ancient feeling. Play slowly at first to feel the modal quality; don't rush toward the tempo. This tune breathes differently from major-key reels. Henry Reed's LOC recording is essential listening. Let the open strings sustain freely — the droning quality IS the tune.

title: Katy Hill
description: Associated with the Round Peak area of Surry County, North Carolina — one of the richest veins of Old-Time fiddle tradition in America — 'Katy Hill' was named for a hill near the community of Katy in the Blue Ridge foothills. The Round Peak tradition, centered on the fiddle-banjo duets of Tommy Jarrell and Fred Cockerham, is known for its powerful, heavily bowed style that became highly influential in the Old-Time revival of the 1970s.
