notes: Named for a landmark near Galax, Virginia, 'Katy Hill' has the muscular, hard-driving character of the Round Peak tradition. The bow arm should feel strong and grounded. The A part has a satisfying repetition; the B part breaks free. Tommy Jarrell and Fred Cockerham played this one together. Let the open G string drone freely in the A part for a full, powerful sound.

title: Forked Deer
description: Named for the Forked Deer River in western Tennessee, this reel was a staple of the Tennessee contest fiddle tradition. The Forked Deer River — named by early settlers for its Y-shaped bifurcation — runs through Gibson, Madison, and Dyer counties in west Tennessee. The tune appears in early 20th-century fiddle contest records and was widely played in the Mississippi Delta and surrounding areas.
notes: A powerful D major reel with a characteristic hook in the A part that listeners remember immediately. The 'fork' in the title is reflected in the tune's structure — phrases that split and rejoin. Keep the bow arm strong and steady; this is not a delicate tune. The B part rises and falls dramatically. At Tennessee contests this was a staple that fiddlers used to showcase their command of the bow.

title: Flop-Eared Mule
description: A comic fiddle tune from the Southern tradition, 'Flop-Eared Mule' belongs to the category of animal-named tunes that were popular at 19th-century dances and social gatherings — 'Old Grey Mule,' 'Kickin' Mule,' 'Hell Among the Yearlings.' The mule was the workhorse of Southern agriculture, and its cantankerous personality made it a natural subject for folk humor. The tune's unpredictable rhythm reflects the animal's stubborn character.
tags: humorous, G major, family music, dance
notes: A humorous tune named for a mule with drooping ears — play it with that same ornery, unpredictable energy. The rhythm has a slight hitch to it; don't smooth it out too much. Great for parties and dances where the audience wants something fun. The open-string drones give it a raw, outdoor quality. Many fiddlers add a 'mule bray' ornament somewhere in the B part.

title: Big Scioty
description: Named for the Scioto River (pronounced 'sy-OH-tuh') in central Ohio, 'Big Scioty' is a tune from the Midwest fiddle tradition. The Scioto Valley was one of the first regions of Ohio settled by pioneers coming from Virginia and Kentucky in the early 1800s — they brought their Appalachian fiddle traditions with them, adapting them to Midwestern contest and dance hall settings. The tune appeared in early Ohio fiddle contest records.
tags: ohio, scioto river, rolling, G major
notes: An Ohio fiddle tune with a broad, rolling character — the 'big' in the name should be in the playing. The Scioto River Valley was the heart of Ohio's early settlement, and this tune has the confident stride of a prosperous agricultural community. Keep the tempo moderate and the bow arm relaxed but firm. Works beautifully in a bluegrass or Old-Time context.

title: Whistle Daughter Whistle
description: A traditional song-and-dance tune of British origin that entered the American folk tradition through the 18th-century immigration period, 'Whistle Daughter Whistle' belongs to the comic song category where children and parents negotiate amusingly. The whistling tradition was an important musical skill in pre-instrument rural communities — field hollers, work signals, and entertainment all relied on the whistled voice. The tune was collected in multiple American versions by Cecil Sharp and later by Alan Lomax.
notes: A song-tune with a comic premise — a daughter who won't whistle until she gets something in return. The playful, negotiating energy should come through in the rhythm. Keep it light and bouncy. The simple pentatonic melody makes it accessible for beginners while the song character gives experienced players room for storytelling.

title: Mississippi Moon
description: The Mississippi River — 2,340 miles from Minnesota to the Gulf of Mexico — is the great artery of American geography and imagination. Its moonlit surface appears in countless American songs, from Stephen Foster ('Beautiful Dreamer') to Mark Twain's descriptions in 'Life on the Mississippi' (1883) to Delta blues recordings. The waltz form — slower, more romantic than a reel — perfectly suits the languid, vast quality of the great river at night.
notes: A waltz with the wide, slow sweep of a Southern river under a full moon — let the bow float with maximum length and minimal pressure. The 3/4 time should feel absolutely natural and expansive. Don't rush; the Mississippi moves slowly. This is a tune where tone quality is everything — a singing, sustained sound in the upper register.

title: Colored Aristocracy
description: A Missouri breakdown from the post-Civil War era. The bright D major melody contrasts with the fraught history of its title.
tags: missouri, civil war era, D major, historical

title: John Henry Blues
description: John Henry is the great American labor hero — a Black railroad worker who is said to have driven steel faster than a steam hammer at the Big Bend Tunnel on the Chesapeake & Ohio Railway in West Virginia around 1870, then died of exhaustion. The story, whether historical or mythological, became one of the most widely recorded songs in American music. John Henry represented Black workers' dignity, strength, and resistance to industrial dehumanization. Guy Johnson's 1929 study 'John Henry: Tracking Down a Negro Legend' began the scholarly inquiry that continues today.
tags: john henry, blues, folk hero, G major
notes: One of America's great folk heroes — play this with the weight and resolve of a steel-driver. The blues quality should come through in the slightly bent notes and the heavy rhythmic pulse. Don't play this light; John Henry died swinging a hammer, and the music should carry that gravity. A slow-to-medium tempo reveals the character.

title: If I Hadn't Been A Fool
Hold Old Bald While I Dance With Josie
Abe's Retreat
description: Political commentary through fiddle tune titles was a long tradition in American folk music. 'Abe's Retreat' — naming a tune for Abraham Lincoln's supposed retreat from something — suggests Southern or anti-Lincoln origin in the Civil War era. Whether sincere political commentary or ironic nickname, the title places the tune in the contentious political culture of mid-19th century America. Many Civil War-era tunes used political figures' names as coded commentary on events of the day.
notes: A tongue-in-cheek political tune — 'Abe' is presumably Lincoln, and 'retreat' was the last thing Lincoln did. Play it with some irony and forward momentum. The breakdown character suits a moderate-to-fast tempo. A historically interesting tune whose title suggests it may have originated in Confederate-sympathizing communities.

title: Altamont
description: Altamont is a common Appalachian place name — meaning 'high mountain' — appearing in multiple Southern states. The tune is associated with the Galax, Virginia fiddle tradition and has circulated in Old-Time and bluegrass contests since at least the mid-20th century. North Carolina and Virginia fiddlers associated with the Galax region developed a clean, driving contest style that this tune exemplifies.
notes: A fast, bright reel from the Southern contest tradition — 'Altamont' suggests elevation and clear mountain air. Keep the bow arm confident and the tempo driving. This tune rewards careful attention to bow distribution across the phrase. Good for demonstrating clean string crossings at speed. At North Carolina contests it's often played at a blinding tempo.

title: (And) The Cat Came Back
description: Written in 1893 by Tin Pan Alley composer Harry S. Miller and published in Chicago by Will Rossiter, 'The Cat Came Back' began as a darkly comic novelty song with minstrel staging and problematic racial dialect. Its core premise — 'Old Mister Johnson' tries every increasingly absurd method to rid himself of a persistent yellow cat, and the cat returns each time — proved irresistibly funny and the song's structure, with its relentless chorus, gave it enormous staying power. The tune migrated into children's music, folk revival repertoires, and eventually old-time fiddle sessions, losing its minstrel origins along the way and becoming simply one of the great comic songs of American tradition. Fred Penner's 1979 children's recording introduced it to multiple new generations. The fiddle tune derived from the song retains the rhythmic bounce and inevitable return of the melody — the musical equivalent of the cat's refusal to stay gone.
notes: The melody's built-in humor is the whole point. The 'return' figure — when the melody circles back to the main theme — should feel inevitable and funny every time. D major, bright and bouncy. Great for singalongs: 'But the cat came back, the very next day / Thought it was a goner but the cat came back.' Don't overthink it. This is joy music.

title: Antelope Gap
description: Preserved through the playing of Texas fiddlers Howard Rains and Trish Spencer, who documented it on their recording 'Old Texas Fiddle,' 'Antelope Gap' is attributed to Texas fiddler J.W. Whatley. The tune found an unlikely second home in the Tucson, Arizona old-time jam scene, where it became a local favorite without spreading widely elsewhere — a reminder that regional tune ecosystems develop their own peculiar repertoires. Antelope Gap is a real geographic feature: a pass through ridgelines common in the American West, usually named for the pronghorn antelope that would funnel through such natural channels. Texas fiddle tradition draws from Appalachian, Cajun, and western swing influences, and tunes like 'Antelope Gap' sit in the overlap — rhythmically driving without the modal darkness of the deepest Appalachian repertoire.
notes: A major with a Texas-style drive — keep the bow moving and don't let it breathe too much. The tune has a straightforward AABB structure without the modal ambiguity of Kentucky or Virginia styles. Howard Rains and Trish Spencer's recording on 'Old Texas Fiddle' is the primary reference. Good for sessions that want Texas flavor between Appalachian sets.

title: Apple Blossom
description: Apple orchards were a cornerstone of Appalachian farm economies — apple butter, cider, dried apples, and apple brandy ('apple jack') were essential preserved foods and trade goods. The brief apple blossom period in late spring, when hillside orchards turned white and pink, was one of the most celebrated moments of the Appalachian seasonal calendar. Old-Time waltzes often carry the names of natural phenomena that marked the agricultural year.
notes: A waltz with the delicate, brief beauty of apple blossoms — play it lightly and without pressing the bow. The 3/4 time should float. Apple orchards were central to Appalachian farm life, and their brief spring bloom was a celebrated seasonal event. Keep the tempo unhurried and the tone as sweet as possible.

title: Apple Jack
description: 'Apple Jack' belongs to the large family of Appalachian breakdown tunes named for foods, drinks, and rural materials — a tradition that includes 'Cornbread and Buttermilk,' 'Sugar in the Gourd,' and dozens of others. Applejack — a fermented and distilled apple beverage that was the primary liquor of many mountain communities before commercial whiskey became widely available — was produced across the Appalachian region from the 17th century onward, especially in Virginia, New Jersey, and the Carolinas. The drink appears in numerous folk songs and references as a symbol of frontier self-sufficiency and social gathering. The tune itself is a rhythmic breakdown in the standard old-time AABB form, passed down through the oral tradition of Appalachian musicians whose names and specific origins are no longer traceable.
notes: C major breakdown with the driving quality that characterized Appalachian dance music. The two-part AABB structure is clear and symmetrical, making it easy to jam with first-time partners who can learn the form quickly. The name suggests something strong and slightly rough around the edges, which should inform your bow arm: pressure and confidence rather than delicacy.

title: Arrington's Breakdown
description: Named for Charlie Arrington, an in-demand studio and dance musician of the 1920s–30s who recorded prolifically during the first golden era of old-time recording. Arrington was a working fiddler in the Southern professional music world — playing dances, recording sessions, and bandstands — and his breakdown reflects the polished, driving style of musicians who needed to hold a crowd and a dance floor night after night. The tune was preserved in the oral tradition and documented by modern fiddlers including Chirps Smith (who learned it from Paul Tyler) and the Volo Bogtrotters. Like many named breakdowns, it represents the practice of naming tunes for the fiddler who popularized them rather than necessarily who composed them — attribution in the oral tradition was often about the best-known carrier rather than the original inventor.
notes: G major breakdown with a driving, danceable rhythm. Play it with confidence and a hard bow — this is professional dance music, not a contemplative piece. The structure is clear AABB. A good tune for building bow arm endurance because the rhythmic demands are constant. Learn the version from Chirps Smith's recordings if you can find them.

title: Backstep Cindy
description: One of the most beloved tunes from the Round Peak tradition of Surry County, North Carolina, 'Backstep Cindy' is a three-part crooked tune played in high-bass tuning (ADAE — the G string raised a whole step to A). The Round Peak style, centered around the musical community of Tommy Jarrell, Fred Cockerham, and their neighbors, is characterized by heavy bow pressure, drone-string emphasis, and a rhythmic drive that prioritizes dancing over prettiness. 'Backstep Cindy' exemplifies these values: its irregular phrase lengths ('crooked phrasing') create a rhythmic surprise that experienced old-time dancers specifically enjoy, while the ADAE tuning opens up drone possibilities unavailable in standard tuning. The title's 'Cindy' connects it to the vast family of Appalachian dance songs featuring female names — Cindy, Sally, Nellie, Betsy — most of which circulated as both song and tune in overlapping communities. 'Get along home, Cindy Cindy / Get along home, I say' is the lyrical world the tune inhabits.
notes: Tune up before you start: ADAE puts the G string up a whole step, which gives you a ringing open A as the bass drone. The three parts (A, B, C) each have slightly different phrase lengths — don't try to regularize them. Let the crookedness happen. Play with the weight and bow pressure of Round Peak style: closer to the bridge, slower bow strokes than you think, more volume than you expect. A foundational tune for anyone learning the Round Peak tradition.

title: (On The) Banks Of The Ohio
description: One of the most recorded murder ballads in American folk music, 'Banks of the Ohio' tells the story of a young man who drowns a woman when she refuses to marry him. The earliest known recording was by Red Patterson's Piedmont Log Rollers in 1927; the ballad itself is anonymous and likely dates from the mid-to-late 19th century, circulating through oral tradition for decades before anyone pressed it to wax. Like many Appalachian murder ballads, it presents the killer's perspective without moral judgment, leaving the listener to supply the outrage. 'I asked my love to take a walk / to take a walk just a little walk / Down beside where the waters flow / Down by the banks of the Ohio' — the language is pastoral, almost tender, which makes the murder more disturbing. Bill Monroe, Olivia Newton-John, Emmylou Harris, Doc Watson, and dozens of others have recorded it. The Ohio River, which forms the boundary between Kentucky and Ohio, was a real and symbolically powerful geographic feature in the 19th-century American imagination — the line between slave and free states.
notes: A minor or D minor depending on the version, though many singers use C major for a brighter, more unsettling contrast with the dark text. The tune is a song-tune: let the melody breathe, follow the text rhythm, and don't rush the long notes. The fiddle version works well as an introductory solo before vocals, or as a slow dance tune. The simplicity of the melody is its strength — don't ornament it to death.

title: Battle of Cedar Creek
description: The Battle of Cedar Creek (October 19, 1864) was a major engagement in the Shenandoah Valley of Virginia, in which Union General Philip Sheridan rallied his army from near-defeat to a decisive victory over Confederate General Jubal Early. Sheridan's famous 'ride from Winchester' — twenty miles to reach his retreating troops — became an instant legend. Civil War battles in the Shenandoah Valley directly affected the fiddle communities of the region, and the war's memory permeated Old-Time music for generations.
notes: A march-like breakdown commemorating a Civil War battle — keep the rhythm military-steady and the tempo moderate. The A part has a marching quality; the B part adds some melodic relief. Don't rush; this is a commemoration, not a celebration. Let the weight of the history come through in the playing.

title: Beaux Of Albany
description: 'Beaux of Albany' traces its roots to an 18th-century Scottish reel that made its way across the Atlantic and took root in the New England contra dance tradition before spreading south into the broader American fiddle repertoire. The Scottish original appeared under titles including 'The Braes of Auchtertyre' in collections from the 1740s onward. Its transformation into the American 'Beaux of Albany' — Albany being the capital of New York, a significant urban center in the early republic — likely occurred as the tune circulated through New England dance halls and meeting houses in the late 18th and early 19th centuries. The tune belongs to the 'reel' family that formed the backbone of New England contra dance music, characterized by clear 8-bar strains, symmetrical phrasing, and a drive suitable for long-formation dances with many couples. Its D-major setting gives it a bright, formal quality that suits its association with a city rather than a hollow or a creek.
notes: D major with the characteristic brightness and forward motion of a New England reel. The AABB structure is textbook — clear, predictable, and danceable. This is a good contra dance tune: the phrases are even enough for callers to work with and the energy sustains across many repetitions. If you're coming from an old-time or Appalachian background, the New England styling — slightly more 'civilized' than a mountain breakdown — asks for precise bow placement and clean string crossings.

title: Belle of Lexington
description: Despite its name suggesting Kentucky's horse-country capital, 'Belle of Lexington' is primarily associated with southwestern Virginia — specifically Grayson and Carroll Counties, the same densely musical region that produced Albert Hash, Thornton Spencer, and the broader Whitetop Mountain musical community. The definitive recording came from Emmett Lundy (1864–1953), the legendary Grayson County fiddler, who cut it as 'Belles of Lexington.' Lundy's archaic, powerful style preserved melodic and rhythmic elements that other fiddlers of the commercial era had smoothed away, making his recordings essential documents of pre-commercial Appalachian music. The tune belongs to the 'Smith's Reel' family and shares melodic material with the Irish hornpipe 'Kitty's Wedding' and the related titles 'Belle Election' and 'Hauling Home.' This Irish connection is typical of the Appalachian repertoire, where tunes crossed the Atlantic and then spent a century or more diverging from their source material.
notes: Emmett Lundy's recording is the primary reference and worth finding and studying. The tune has a formal elegance — a 'belle,' after all, suggests something refined — but Lundy played it with Appalachian grit that contradicts the prettiness of the title. F major with some chromatic inflections in certain versions. The B part has an Irish reel character that's fun to lean into. Let the bow arm drive.

title: Betty Baker (Over the Hill to Betty Baker)
Bibb County Hoedown
description: Bibb County, Georgia was named for William Wyatt Bibb, Georgia's first governor (1817). Located in central Georgia with Macon as its county seat, Bibb County was part of the fertile Georgia piedmont that supported a prosperous agricultural economy. The 'hoedown' — originally a dance where participants stamped and clapped rhythmically — became a generic term for any vigorous country dance gathering. Georgia fiddle contest traditions were distinct from both Virginia and Texas styles.
notes: A Georgia breakdown with a strong, county-fair energy. Keep the bow arm driving and the rhythm absolutely steady. A hoedown was literally a dance at a farm gathering — communal, informal, and exuberant. This tune should feel like a crowd of people who've been working hard and are ready to dance hard too.

title: Big Eyed Rabbit
description: Animal-themed tunes were among the most popular in the Old-Time repertoire — 'Big Eyed Rabbit,' 'Rabbit in the Pea Patch,' 'Rabbit Where'd You Get Them Long Ears' — reflecting the rabbit's prominent place in both Appalachian hunting culture and African American trickster tales (Br'er Rabbit). The rabbit was a dietary staple and a figure of folk wisdom: always watchful, always ready to run, surviving through cleverness rather than strength.
notes: A comic, animal-themed breakdown with a loose, swinging quality. The rabbit's wide eyes suggest wariness and speed — keep the rhythm quick and light. Don't dig the bow in; let it bounce. This is one of those tunes that sounds better played with a little carelessness than with excessive precision. Great for large sessions.

title: Bitter Creek
description: Bitter Creek could refer to several geographic features in the American West and South — there are Bitter Creeks in Wyoming, West Virginia, and elsewhere — all named because their water was alkaline, sulfurous, or otherwise undrinkable. In Appalachian folklore, 'bitter' was used to describe situations or places that were genuinely difficult — bitter cold, bitter grief, bitter labor. Old-Time tunes with austere names often preserved an unflinching honesty about the hardships of rural life.
notes: A tune with an uncompromising name — 'bitter' in Appalachian parlance meant something difficult, hard, or genuinely unpleasant. Play it with some grit and don't try to sweeten it up. The modal quality enhances the sense of hardship. A tune that tells the truth about difficult experiences without melodrama.

title: Black-Eyed Susie
description: The black-eyed Susan (Rudbeckia hirta) is a wildflower native to eastern North America — its bright yellow petals and dark center made it one of the most recognizable flowers of the Appalachian meadow landscape. In Old-Time tradition, 'Black-Eyed Susie' refers to a young woman, likely dark-eyed and attractive. The tune appears in multiple collections from across the Appalachian region and has been recorded by dozens of artists from traditional fiddlers to modern string bands.
notes: A cheerful courting tune that's one of the most widely-played in the Old-Time tradition. Keep it bright and forward. The A part has an insistent, questioning quality; the B part answers with more confidence. This tune is great for beginners because the form is clear and forgiving, but it has enough character to reward advanced players who add ornamentation.

title: Black Satin
description: Satin — a smooth, glossy woven fabric with a silky texture — was a luxury textile associated with formal dress, ballrooms, and high-status social occasions in 19th-century American culture. 'Black Satin' as a tune name evokes the world of formal social dancing: polished floors, fine clothes, and carefully executed dance figures. The tune's smooth melodic character suits the material it's named for.
notes: A smooth, elegant tune that should sound like its name — silky and polished. Keep the bow arm relaxed and the tone round and warm. No roughness here. This is a tune for showing off clean intonation and smooth bow changes. Play it at a moderate tempo where the elegance can register.

title: Blue Goose
description: The snow goose (Chen caerulescens) has a blue-gray 'blue morph' phase that gave it the folk name 'blue goose' in many parts of North America. Migratory waterfowl — geese, ducks, herons — were important food sources and harbingers of seasonal change in Appalachian culture. The Blue Goose was also a common name for country stores and roadhouses throughout the rural South, suggesting a warm, unpretentious gathering place.
notes: A tune with the unhurried, heavy quality of a goose in flight — keep the tempo moderate and the bow arm grounded. The Blue Goose was a real bird and a real brand, and the name suggests something solid and unpretentious. Don't rush this one. Let the open string drones carry.

title: Boating Up The Sandy
description: The Big Sandy River, forming the border between West Virginia and Kentucky, was a major transportation route in the early 19th century. Before roads and railroads, flatboats and keelboats moved goods along river systems throughout Appalachia. 'Boating up' the river — working upstream against the current — was grueling labor that required organized crews working in rhythm. Work songs and fiddle tunes that matched the rhythm of physical labor were a practical necessity on early American waterways.
notes: A river tune with a powerful, upstream-pulling quality — 'boating up' meant poling or pulling a flatboat against the current. Put that muscle into the bow arm. The rhythm should feel like steady, rhythmic labor. The Sandy River (probably the Big Sandy, West Virginia/Kentucky) was a major commerce route in the early 19th century.

title: Bone Yard
description: A 'bone yard' in American rural parlance was either a cemetery, a place where animal carcasses were disposed of, or a junkyard of discarded machinery — all suggesting the aftermath of death and the long decomposition of material things. The name gives this Old-Time tune a memento mori quality unusual in the fiddle repertoire. Modal tunes with dark titles often preserved older folk practices of naming music for the full spectrum of human (and animal) experience, not just its bright moments.
notes: A tune with a spare, skeletal quality — play it without much ornamentation, letting the bare structure show. The modal quality and open string drones give it an austere, almost eerie feeling. Keep the bow arm relaxed but the rhythm precise. This is a tune that sounds better late at night than at midday.

title: Booth Shot Lincoln
description: John Wilkes Booth shot President Abraham Lincoln at Ford's Theatre in Washington, DC on April 14, 1865 — five days after General Lee's surrender at Appomattox. Lincoln died the following morning. The assassination shocked the nation and transformed Reconstruction policy. That this event became the title of a fiddle tune reflects how deeply it penetrated popular consciousness — and how Old-Time music encoded American history in its repertoire. The tune circulated in both Northern and Southern communities with very different emotional valences.
notes: The most historically charged title in the Old-Time fiddle canon. Play it with the weight that event deserves — an event that changed American history on April 14, 1865. The minor-tinged quality should feel somber without being melodramatic. A tune that makes audiences stop and think.

title: Bound to Have a Little Fun
description: 'Bound to Have a Little Fun' belongs to the category of Old-Time tunes that are essentially mission statements — announcing their purpose in the title. In the context of pre-radio Appalachian life, where entertainment had to be created rather than consumed, the determination to have fun was not trivial. Dance gatherings, music sessions, and community events were hard-won pleasures that required planning and effort. The tune celebrates that determination with unabashed joy.
notes: A tune whose title is its entire philosophy — play it with that determined, unrepentant joy. The rhythm should feel irrepressible. This is not a tune for careful, reserved playing; it's a tune for maximum enjoyment. If the bow arm isn't having fun, start over. A perfect session closer when everyone is warmed up.

title: Breaking Up Christmas
description: In Appalachian tradition, 'Christmas' extended from December 25 through January 6 (Old Christmas or Epiphany) — a twelve-day season of visiting, feasting, and dancing. 'Breaking up Christmas' was the final community dance that ended this extended holiday, marking the return to ordinary work life. The tradition was strongest in Virginia and North Carolina; folklorist Patrick Mullen documented the custom in detail. The tune carries both the festivity of Christmas and the melancholy of its ending.
notes: One of the most evocatively named tunes in the Old-Time tradition — 'breaking up Christmas' refers to the end of the holiday season, when neighbors gathered one last time for dancing and music. Play it with the festive, slightly bittersweet energy of a party ending. A strong, driving tempo is traditional.

title: Buckskin Reel
description: Buckskin — deer leather tanned using the deer's own brain — was the primary clothing material for Native American peoples and early European frontiersmen throughout North America. Daniel Boone, Davy Crockett, and other frontier heroes were depicted in buckskin in popular imagery. By the 19th century, 'buckskin' had become synonymous with frontier self-reliance and practical craftsmanship. Tunes with frontier-clothing names — buckskin, linsey-woolsey, homespun — evoked the aesthetic of practical self-sufficiency.
notes: A frontier-energy tune — buckskin (tanned deer leather) was the quintessential clothing material of the American frontier. Play it with the direct, unadorned quality of buckskin itself: no frills, just function. The rhythm should be solid and dependable. A good all-purpose session tune that works at any tempo.

title: Bull of the Woods
description: In Southern logging camp culture, the 'bull of the woods' was the woods foreman — the authority figure who commanded the logging crew and set the pace of work. Logging was one of the most physically demanding and dangerous occupations in Appalachia, and the social hierarchy of the logging camp was intensely masculine. Tunes named for logging figures and activities — 'Bull of the Woods,' 'Lumberjack Polka,' 'The Logger's Boast' — commemorated this important regional industry.
notes: A powerful, dominant-energy tune — the bull of the woods was the biggest, strongest man on a logging crew, and this tune should feel like him. Keep the bow arm heavy and confident. The rhythm should be absolutely unshakeable. A great tune for demonstrating strong tone production and a commanding presence.

title: Bye Bye My Honey I'm Gone
By The Waterfall
description: Waterfalls were sacred and recreational sites in Appalachian culture — sources of water power, swimming holes in summer, and objects of aesthetic wonder. The Appalachian mountains contain hundreds of significant waterfalls, from Looking Glass Falls in North Carolina to Blackwater Falls in West Virginia. In the Romantic tradition that permeated 19th-century American culture, waterfalls represented the sublime — the overwhelming power and beauty of nature that humans could witness but not control.
notes: A meditative, flowing tune — let the bow arm mirror the water's movement. Long, smooth strokes work better than short, detached ones. The waterfall setting suggests both beauty and power; the music should have both qualities. Play slowly enough to hear the individual notes sustain and blend. A tune that rewards patience.

title: Caliche Creek
description: Caliche (pronounced ka-LEE-chee) is the hardpan calcium carbonate layer found just below the surface in arid and semi-arid soils across the American Southwest, Great Plains, and parts of Texas. For farmers and ranchers, caliche was a genuine obstacle — too hard to plow through, impeding drainage and root growth. Creeks flowing through caliche country had a distinctive milky appearance. The tune likely originated in the Texas fiddle tradition, which developed its own distinct character from Appalachian styles.
notes: A Southwest-inflected tune — caliche is the calcium carbonate crust that forms in arid soils of the American Southwest and Great Plains. Play with a slightly different character than Appalachian creek tunes: drier, more open, with less of the lush mountain sound. A tune that feels like a different landscape.

title: Calico Corn
description: Calico corn — also called Indian corn, flint corn, or ornamental corn — is a heritage variety of maize with multi-colored kernels in patterns of purple, red, yellow, blue, and white. It was grown by Native American peoples throughout North America and adopted by European settlers who used it for food (cornmeal, hominy), animal feed, and decoration. The autumn harvest of calico corn was a communal activity that culminated in corn-shucking parties — community events with music, food, and dancing.
notes: A cheerful, harvest-time breakdown — calico corn (multi-colored Indian corn) was both a food crop and a decorative autumn staple. Keep the rhythm bright and energetic. This is a tune for the harvest dance, played after the corn is in the crib and the hard work is done. Let the bow bounce.

title: Camp Chase
description: Camp Chase in Columbus, Ohio was a Union prisoner-of-war camp that held Confederate soldiers from 1861 to 1865. At its peak it held 8,000–9,000 prisoners in conditions that were desperately overcrowded; approximately 2,260 Confederate soldiers died there, mainly from disease. The camp cemetery still exists in Columbus. Tunes named for Civil War camps — Camp Chase, Camp Douglas, Andersonville — carried the weight of that experience for the communities that lost men to those places.
notes: A reflective, minor-tinged tune named for one of the Civil War's notorious Northern prisoner-of-war camps. Play it with restraint and gravity — this is a tune about confinement and suffering. The melody has a quality of quiet endurance. Let the phrases breathe and don't rush the resolution.

title: Camp Meeting on the Fourth of July
description: Camp meeting revivals were a central institution of 19th-century American religious life — outdoor gatherings lasting days or weeks where preachers, musicians, and thousands of worshippers camped together for an extended period of communal prayer and conversion. The Fourth of July was often chosen for camp meetings because it maximized attendance. The combination — patriotism and evangelical religion — captured two of the most powerful currents in 19th-century American culture and the music that expressed both.
notes: A joyful, celebratory breakdown combining two great American institutions: the camp meeting revival and Independence Day. Play it with maximum energy and enthusiasm. This tune should feel like 300 people clapping and singing in a field. Don't hold back — this is a tune about unreserved collective joy.

title: (Old) Cheat Mountain
description: Cheat Mountain in Randolph County, West Virginia rises to 4,848 feet — one of the highest peaks in the state. The Cheat River (which the mountain takes its name from) was reputedly named for its treacherous nature, which 'cheated' travelers who tried to ford it. Civil War skirmishing occurred on Cheat Mountain in 1861 in one of Robert E. Lee's first campaigns as a Confederate general. The area remained remote and wild well into the 20th century, home to a rich fiddle tradition.
notes: A mountain breakdown with a slightly deceptive quality built into its name — the Cheat Mountain area of West Virginia was wild, remote, and treacherous country. Play it with a slightly unpredictable energy. The rhythm should feel secure but not completely square. This tune rewards fiddlers who can play with confident looseness.

title: Cuckoo's Nest
description: 'Cuckoo's Nest' is among the oldest tunes in the English-speaking world's folk repertoire, with documented appearances dating to at least the early 18th century across multiple traditions simultaneously. In England, it survives as a Cotswold Morris dance tune associated with villages including Bledington, Ilmington, and Longborough — some scholars date its Morris use to the mid-17th century. In Scotland, it appears as a reel under the same name, with attribution theories pointing to Scottish origins. It crossed the Atlantic with Scots-Irish immigrants and entered the American old-time repertoire, where it appears in regional collections throughout the 19th century. The cuckoo of the title carries both ornithological meaning (the cuckoo was the harbinger of spring in British folk tradition) and bawdy implication — 'cuckoo's nest' was a common euphemism in 18th-century popular songs, and the playful energy of the tune suits both readings. Its universality — Morris dance, Scottish session, Appalachian breakdown, New England contra dance — makes it one of the most cross-traditional tunes in the English-speaking world.
notes: D major with a bright, rollicking quality that has made it a crowd-pleaser across three centuries and two continents. The AABB structure is symmetrical and easy to pick up, which is why it works in so many different dance contexts. The American old-time version tends to drive harder and sit lower in the bow arm than the English Morris or Scottish session versions. Learn all three if you can — the interpretive differences reveal how the same melody can serve completely different musical communities.

title: Davey Come Back and Act Like You Oughta
Dean Reed's Favorite (Oh How She Lied)
Dog Treed A Possum Up A White Oak Tree
Feed My Horse Corn and Hay
Forty Miles From Georgetown Without Any Whiskey
Getting Out of the Way of the Federals
Going to the Wedding to Get Some Cake
Goodbye Girls I'm Going To Boston
Hanging Around the Kitchen Until the Cook Comes Home
Hop High Ladies
description: 'Hop High Ladies' is the American old-time descendant of 'Miss McLeod's Reel,' a Scottish reel that dates to the early 19th century or earlier. The primary melodic difference between the two is telling: the Scottish original ends phrases on the dominant (a harmonically open, questioning gesture), while the American version resolves to the tonic (settled, complete). This subtle shift transforms the feel of the tune from one of anticipation to one of satisfaction — fitting, perhaps, for the communal American dance tradition that adapted it. The tune's famous command — 'Hop high ladies, step lively too / Hop high ladies, the cake's all through' — connects it to the cakewalk tradition of Southern community dances, where the best dancers won a prize. Early recordings include versions by New England fiddlers, Appalachian string bands, and Midwestern dance orchestras, showing how thoroughly the tune permeated American folk music culture.
notes: D major with a light, skipping quality that matches the 'hopping' of the title. The American version should feel grounded and complete — land on the tonic. The Scottish Miss McLeod's version, if you know it, will feel different by comparison. Good for singalongs: 'Hop high ladies the cake's all through / Hop high ladies, step lively too.' In dance contexts, the caller can work with the clear four-bar phrases. Keep the tempo brisk but not rushed.

title: I Love My Wife As Well As Anybody...
I'm Gonna Have My Mustache Blacked When I Get There
Jaybird Died of the Whooping Cough
Jenny Run Away in the Mud in the Night
Kickin' Up the Devil on a Holiday
(Missouri) Spotted Pony
description: One of the most popular tunes in the Missouri Ozarks tradition, 'Spotted Pony' has roots in the late 19th century — fiddlers of the early 20th century reported learning it from their grandparents' generation. Folklorist Vance Randolph documented it in his 1954 list of traditional Ozark Mountain fiddle tunes, the most comprehensive survey of the regional repertoire. At least three distinct tunes share the name 'Spotted Pony,' circulating across Missouri, Arkansas, and Texas, which suggests the title was applied to multiple melodies in different communities rather than tracing back to a single source. The image of a spotted pony — piebald, pinto, colorful — was a common metaphor for something lively and unpredictable in Southern rural culture. The tune's rhythmic drive and clear structure made it a staple of Midwestern dances and contests, and it remains one of the tunes most likely to appear in an Ozark-style old-time session.
notes: C major with a rolling, confident structure. The tune sits well under the fingers in first position and has a natural momentum that carries dancers. Multiple versions exist — some with slightly different A parts, some in different keys — so it's worth knowing which version your band plays before the jam. The rhythm should feel light-footed, like the pony of the title. A bright, up-bow stroke on the strong beats gives it energy.

title: Muddy Creek (aka Morgan on the Railroad)
Nail that Catfish to the Tree
Never Mind the Weather When the Wind Don't Blow
Old Aunt Jenny With Her Nightcap On
Ol' Bob
description: A tune from the Kentucky oral tradition associated with Gusty Wallace (1890–1985), a fiddler from Hart County who spent most of his life in Sulphur Well, Metcalfe County, and was recorded by Bruce Greene in 1975. Wallace's version has the irregular phrase lengths and restless multi-part structure (ABCC') that characterize the deeper strata of Appalachian fiddling, where tunes evolved through decades of ear-to-ear transmission with no written score to anchor them. The most widely circulated modern version comes from Garry Harrison's CD 'Red Prairie Dawn,' featuring clawhammer banjo by Paul Brown — a recording that became a primary teaching source for many players entering the tradition in the 2000s. Fiddlers describe it as 'a damned addictive sort of a tune': the irregular bar lengths catch the ear and the melody refuses to leave. The name likely refers to a specific horse or person in the central Kentucky community that gave birth to it, after the old custom of naming tunes for local figures.
notes: The irregular measures are structural, not errors — Gusty Wallace played them that way because that is how the tune lives. Don't try to regularize the phrasing. Learn to feel where the extra beat falls and let it land. G major with open-string drones gives it a warm, full resonance. Once it gets into your bow arm, it is genuinely hard to shake.

title: Old Time Billy in the Lowground
Old Time Fire on the Mountain
On The Banks Of The Kaney
Over The Stump And Back Again
Paddy Won't You Drink Some Good Old Cider
Poor Little Johnny's Gone To War
Sail Away Ladies
description: 'Sail Away Ladies' has deep roots in south-central Kentucky and middle Tennessee, with the melody tracing back to the 'Sally Ann' family of tunes and their British Isles antecedents. The earliest recorded version is Uncle Bunt Stevens's 1926 instrumental fiddle recording — purely instrumental, no lyrics. Uncle Dave Macon's 1927 recording added the song's most famous lyrics: 'Ain't nobody's business but my own / Sail away ladies, sail away.' Macon — the 'Dixie Dewdrop,' one of the original Grand Ole Opry stars — gave the tune its commercial identity, but it was already a community property well before he touched it. The image of 'sailing away' in the context of a Kentucky or Tennessee mountain song is striking: the nearest navigable water was far enough away that sailing was a metaphor for escape and liberation rather than a description of actual travel. That distance between the lyric and the physical reality gives the song its particular flavor of longing. The tune has been recorded by Flatt and Scruggs, the New Lost City Ramblers, and dozens of revival-era artists.
notes: G major with a driving, optimistic rhythm that belies any sadness in the lyric. The four-part structure (AABBCCDD in some versions) gives the tune more variety than a standard two-part breakdown. Sing it while you play: 'Sail away ladies, sail away.' Uncle Dave Macon's banjo version is the canonical reference for the song tradition; for fiddle, Bunk Stevens's clean instrumental version is the starting point. Good tune for set openings because the rhythm is immediately engaging.

title: Sal's Got Mud Between Her Toes
Spotted Pony
description: One of the most popular tunes in the Missouri Ozarks tradition, 'Spotted Pony' has roots in the late 19th century — fiddlers of the early 20th century reported learning it from their grandparents' generation. Folklorist Vance Randolph documented it in his 1954 list of traditional Ozark Mountain fiddle tunes, the most comprehensive survey of the regional repertoire. At least three distinct tunes share the name 'Spotted Pony,' circulating across Missouri, Arkansas, and Texas, which suggests the title was applied to multiple melodies in different communities rather than tracing back to a single source. The image of a spotted pony — piebald, pinto, colorful — was a common metaphor for something lively and unpredictable in Southern rural culture. The tune's rhythmic drive and clear structure made it a staple of Midwestern dances and contests, and it remains one of the tunes most likely to appear in an Ozark-style old-time session.
notes: C major with a rolling, confident structure. The tune sits well under the fingers in first position and has a natural momentum that carries dancers. Multiple versions exist — some with slightly different A parts, some in different keys — so it's worth knowing which version your band plays before the jam. The rhythm should feel light-footed, like the pony of the title. A bright, up-bow stroke on the strong beats gives it energy.

title: Streak O' Lean Streak O' Fat
The Tune The Old Cow Died On
22nd of February
description: Composed by Zeke Backus and first released by Snuffy Jenkins and The Hired Hands in 1962, '22nd of February' takes its name from George Washington's birthday, which was designated a federal holiday in 1879 and remained a major celebratory occasion in rural American communities well into the 20th century. Folklorist Alan Jabbour theorized that the closely related tune '28th of January' — named for the Battle of New Orleans anniversary — shares common roots with '22nd of February,' and that calendar-named tunes may represent a tradition of commemorating civic occasions through fiddle music. This connection between patriotic holidays and fiddle repertoire was more common in the 19th and early 20th centuries, when local celebrations often included community dances. Also known as 'Miller's Reel,' the tune demonstrates how the same melody could accumulate multiple titles as it moved through different communities and contexts.
notes: A major with a bright, celebratory quality suited to its patriotic title. The tune has clear AABB structure and a rhythm that suggests lively dancing. Related tunes '28th of January' and 'Miller's Reel' are worth knowing if you learn this one — the family resemblance is clear once you play all three. Snuffy Jenkins's banjo recording is the primary reference; the tune has a slightly different energy in fiddle arrangements.

title: Walk Chalk Chicken with a Necktie On
Walking in My Sleep
description: A Blue Ridge breakdown from the Round Peak heartland of Surry County, North Carolina and Patrick County, Virginia, 'Walking in My Sleep' carries the loose, ragtime-inflected quality that characterizes some of the most interesting tunes in the Tommy Jarrell and Fred Cockerham repertoire. The tune has a 'rag-like' melody — syncopated, slightly swinging — that suggests the influence of early 20th-century popular music on the mountain tradition, a reminder that Appalachian fiddlers were not isolated from commercial music but absorbed and transformed it constantly. The dreamlike quality of the title — walking in one's sleep, moving without full consciousness — resonates with the tune's slightly off-kilter rhythm, which seems to hover between full wakefulness and something looser. Collected from the Round Peak tradition, it appears in fiddle recordings and instructional material associated with the Surry County musical community.
notes: G major with a rag-like syncopation that requires careful rhythmic attention — the accents don't always fall where you expect them. Play it with Round Peak bow weight: pressure, commitment, drones ringing. Don't iron out the syncopation trying to make it 'regular.' The irregularity is the charm. Medium tempo where the rhythmic interest is audible; too fast and you lose the rag-like feel that makes this tune distinctive.

title: Who Hit Nellie with the Stovepipe
Quickstep in the Battle of Prague
I Buried My Wife and Danced on Her Grave
R. Aim's Compliments to J. Craigie
DeDannan Polka Set (Julia Clifford's/O'Keefe's Polka/Johnny I Do Miss You)
Niel Gow's Lament on the Death of His Second Wife
Down By The Old Garden Gate
Mi Suegra Aprietan Mis Botas Polka
Second Time in San Javier Two Step
Devil's Dream
description: One of the oldest and most widely-played tunes in the Anglo-American fiddle tradition, 'Devil's Dream' appears in printed collections from the early 19th century and was popular on both sides of the Atlantic. Its name may reference the tune's relentless, driving energy — fast-moving phrases that challenge the player. Documented in Ryan's Mammoth Collection (1883) and numerous New England and Southern fiddle collections, it crossed genre lines into contra dance, square dance, and later Western swing. Tommy Jackson, Doc Roberts, and the New England caller Ralph Page all used it.
